https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Don’t grow old in Labour’s pensioner-hating Britain
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: You would be foolish to bank on Rachel Reeves’ assurance that the triple lock is safe
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Remember Neil Kinnock? He’s now a Labour elder statesman, big advocate for the EU and cheerleader for the all-new-moderate-sounding and royalist Keir Starmer. But go back 40 years, and he was a hard-Left firebrand, advocating the abolition of the monarchy, leaving the EEC and, get this, protecting the rights of the elderly.
In fact, a sweaty Kinnock, the power behind the hopeless Michael Foot, made a ferocious final speech in the 1983 general election campaign with a furious prediction of what a re-elected Thatcher government would bring. Addressing the voters directly, Kinnock croaked wildly at the climax of his speech: “I warn you not to grow old”.
Well, my goodness, how Labour has changed. Now, the older generation is fair game for the Reds, targeted mercilessly to fund a spending spree on public-sector pay increases and other yet-to-be-revealed lefty horrors. If you wonder where the money might come from to pay off striking train drivers and doctors, look no further than the winter fuel allowance, worth £620 per year to an average couple in their later years.
And with Rachel Reeves licking her lips as she considers which taxes to raise in the autumn, despite numerous pre-election promises that she’ll do no such thing, pensioners are right to fear that any capital they’ve managed to build up after a lifetime of dutiful work and diligent saving will be sucked upon. The inheritance tax threshold is likely to remain exactly where it is, drawing more people into its clutches, and the same goes for the income tax threshold, meaning that more pensioners each year will be paying into the Exchequer. Oh, and if you believe Rachel Reeves’ assurance that the triple lock is safe, you’d better not bank on it.
The more innocent may wonder why Labour, traditionally the party that sought to protect the elderly, is suddenly setting its sights on them. But we don’t need to look all that far for the three equally cynical reasons staring right back at us.
First, unlike train drivers, set now to be paid close to £70,000 a year, pensioners can’t strike. Second, pensioners tend to respect the law – although some seem to have been led astray into Just Stop Oil direct action.
Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, pensioners don’t vote Labour. Or very few of them do. The opposite in fact: these days they prop up the Tories.
Labour, it seems, is determined to punish them for all three factors, particularly the last. Yes, Labour says, you’ve worked all your life, saved hard and are looking forward to a little peace in your final years. But we’ve got some strikers to pay off, so go drown your sorrows with what few pennies you still have left, you nasty wrinkly Tories.
Which brings us back to Kinnock and his “I warn you not to grow old” tirade against Thatcher’s Conservative Party of 1983. It was a powerful speech, and by far the most memorable moment of that campaign. We lapped it up. But little did we realise that he was really predicting life under Keir Starmer’s Labour half a century later.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Massive Attack go green as fans told to walk to gig
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Band make mini-festival in Bristol eco-friendly with measures including vegan-only menu, no disposable vapes, and no car parking
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Massive Attack fans have been told to bring their own water bottles and warned that they will not be able to park their cars at what is promised to be the “greenest” show ever this weekend.
Electric shuttle buses will be provided to bring fans to a mini-festival on Sunday in Bristol, the band’s hometown, which they say will have the lowest carbon footprint of a show of its size.
The band is encouraging 34,000 fans to walk, cycle or use public transport to get to the concert, which will feature several other acts, with tickets starting from £70.
The site at Clifton Downs will be run on electricity from huge batteries, rather than diesel generators that are commonly used during big events, and the band are keeping their fingers crossed that the stage lights stay on.
“I think the only time we’ll know it’s worked is when we walk off stage and there’s been no power cuts in between,” singer Robert Del Naja told the BBC.
The electricity will be provided by Ecotricity, the green energy company run by Dale Vince, a Labour donor.
All food on the site will be vegan, fans are encouraged to bring empty water bottles, and will be given a reusable cup for any drinks they buy inside.
Disposable vapes, which are made of plastic and often discarded with valuable lithium-ion batteries inside, will not be permitted on the site, nor will loose glitter – anyone caught with either will be denied entry and have the items confiscated.
Massive Attack has arranged for special trains to run after the show finishes, when other services would already have ended, and train passengers will have access to a separate bar and toilets on the site.
Tickets have also been prioritised for local residents to cut travel emissions.
Mr Vince, who has also donated to Just Stop Oil in the past, posted a video of himself at the site with one of the giant batteries that will power the site.
“It is a first. An event this size, with this many people, being entirely powered by batteries, without a drop of diesel,” he told the BBC. “That’s the fundamental problem of outdoor events – they run on diesel.
“Twelve million litres of diesel are burned annually in our country to power outdoor events.”
The gig, the band’s first in Bristol for five years, will put into practice the recommendations from a study commissioned by Massive Attack on how live music can go green.
Live concerts and performances generate 405,000 tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions every year, equivalent to about 200,000 cars, according to the study from the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research.
The festival comes after other measures by the band to cut their carbon footprint, such as touring Europe by train in 2019, and they hope to set an example that will be copied by other bands.
Earlier this year, Coldplay said that they had cut their carbon emissions by 59 per cent on their world tour compared to previous events, with measures including a dance floor that creates electricity and cutting their air travel.
The band paused touring in 2017 over environmental concerns, before returning four years later with a more eco-friendly plan, including energy-efficient lighting and sets built with sustainable materials such as bamboo.
Chris Martin said at the time that the band had “no comeback” to the argument they should stop touring to limit emissions, except that “we would really like to”.
He told the BBC: “The people that give us backlash for that kind of thing, for flying, they’re right. So we don’t have any argument against that.”
The O2 arena in London served an entirely vegan menu for concerts by Billie Eilish in 2022, during the popstar’s climate-focused tour.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: RSPCA reported to watchdog after president Chris Packham’s Barclays outburst
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Shadow business minister reports groups associated with TV presenter to Charity Commission
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
The RSPCA has been reported to the charity watchdog over comments made by Chris Packham, its president, urging Barclays customers to set themselves on fire.
The BBC presenter gave a speech earlier this month in which he said that anyone who banked with Barclays should “stick your head in a bucket of fuel and set fire to it”.
Greg Smith, the shadow business minister, reported the RSPCA, as well as the RSPB, of which Packham is vice-president, to the Charity Commission. He wrote to the individual charities demanding that the groups “consider” his position.
He told the organisations that Packham’s words were a “deeply damaging contribution to the degradation of public discourse”, particularly in the context of recent riots and disorder.
Mr Smith said that both charities should consider whether Packham is a “fit and proper person” to remain in the roles he holds.
Packham, 63, urged people not to bank with financial institutions that invest in “fossil fuels, weapons and poverty” at an Action for Wildlife Day in Derbyshire.
He said: “But, if anyone here is banking with Barclays, then, I suggest you stick your head in a bucket of fuel and set fire to it because you’re burning our planet down. And, it’s time to put this stuff behind us.”
Barclays is Europe’s biggest fossil-fuel backer, according to environmental campaigners, who say it has channelled £186 billion to the industry since 2016.
Mr Smith wrote to the RSPCA on Friday: “In recent weeks, the use of intemperate and inflammatory language has led directly to grave instances of violent public disorder.
“Had Mr Packham’s comments been made during that time in the context of a debate about immigration, it is likely that he would have been subject to arrest.
“That they were instead addressed to a presumably like-minded audience… does not excuse what I believe to have been a deeply damaging contribution to the degradation of the public discourse.”
He added that although Packham was not speaking in his capacity as president or vice-president of the animal charities, the organisations should publicly “condemn” the remarks.
The RSPB distanced itself from the comments made by Packham. A spokesman said: “While he is aligned to our charitable objectives, he also has his own views and opinions on many issues within the conservation sector and beyond, some of which, we as a charity would not necessarily agree with but would not restrict him expressing.”
The RSPCA said it did not “condone” Packham’s comments, but that he was a “much-loved and a well-respected voice for all animals”.
A spokesman said: “We are proud to have him as our president. Chris is passionate about changing the world but words are important, and we don’t condone the comments he made at the Action for Wildlife event.
“While we don’t always agree on everything, we share his desire to create a better world for all animals.”
David Bean, a spokesman for the Countryside Alliance, said: “Mr Packham’s most recent comments are the latest in an escalating series of bizarre histrionics that he has shown no willingness to control.
“The charities that have closely associated with him ought to consider carefully how many lines they can stand by and watch him cross. If they want to avoid the public concluding that they approve of his behaviour, silence is untenable.”
The campaigner’s appearance at the event was not the first instance of controversy surrounding Packham.
He presented a programme in which he questioned whether it was ethically acceptable to break the law in protesting against government climate policies.
Barclays has been the target of several protests in recent months, including by pro-Palestine activists seeking to pressure the bank into cutting its economic ties with Israel.
Barclays said that it is helping to finance the energy transition, and has a clear strategy to become a net zero bank by 2050, including by reducing its financed emissions.
The bank has also said that from 2024 it will no longer provide project finance or other direct finance to energy firms for new oil and gas projects or related infrastructure.
Extinction Rebellion demonstrators have also conducted protests to urge organisations such as the All England Lawn Tennis Club and the University of Cambridge to drop their use of Barclays over the bank’s links to the fossil-fuel industry.
A spokesman for the Charity Commission said: “We are aware of potential concerns about comments made by Chris Packham, the president of the RSPCA and vice-president of the RSPB. We are assessing information to determine if there is a role for the commission.”
Packham has been approached for comment.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Feargal Sharkey to lead mass London rally over Labour’s failure to tackle water pollution
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Singer says ‘everyone who is angry about the state of our water’ should join march to mark end of Starmer’s first 100 days in office
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Feargal Sharkey will lead a mass rally over the Government’s failure to tackle water pollution after its first 100 days in office.
The activist and singer will be joining a wide range of environmental and sporting groups including River Action, Greenpeace, the Wildlife Trusts, British Rowing and British Canoeing for the protest on Oct 26.
The former Undertones frontman said it was time for everyone to demand action from leaders as the campaigners urge members of the public to join the demonstration through central London to Parliament Square.
Stephen Fry, the actor, has also narrated a film ahead of the march to “get Britain’s water off life support”.
The UK has been facing a growing water quality crisis because of a multitude of factors such as ageing water infrastructure, lack of investment from water firms, a growing population, agriculture runoff and industrial pollution.
The cocktail of raw sewage, agricultural waste, chemical pollutants and plastic is presenting increasing risks to human health as well as untold damage to nature.
The March for Clean Water is timed to mark the end of the first 100 days of the Labour Government and comes days before Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ first budget.
The environmental groups said they will watch closely for the Government to commit finance to protect UK waters during the autumn statement on Oct 30.
While the groups welcomed the introduction of a Water Bill in the King’s Speech in July, they said the proposed initiatives are not extensive enough to address the scale of the crisis.
The protesters will therefore call on Sir Keir Starmer to take immediate and decisive action by including a set of measures in the legislation that will end the pollution of Britain’s rivers, lakes and seas.
This includes a plan to address the continuous illegal dumping of raw sewage by the water companies, a full set of solutions to end all other major sources of water pollution, and reforms to the regulatory system, including Ofwat and the Environment Agency, so the law can be effectively enforced against polluters.
Mr Sharkey said: “We call on the Government to end the environmental devastation being inflicted upon our rivers, lakes and seas.
“It stops here, it stops today, it stops now. End pollution, end polluting for profit.
“We call on everyone in the country who is concerned or angry at the state of our waters to join us and march.”
Charles Watson, River Action founder and chair, said: “The initial noises coming out of our new Government regarding cleaning up our filthy waterways, while encouraging, do not nearly go far enough to deal with the scale of the problem they have inherited.
“Nothing short of wholescale reform of our failed regulatory system and comprehensive strategies to address all major sources of pollution, including sewage discharges and agricultural run-off, will suffice.”
River Action is coordinating the march in collaboration with other groups, which include Surfers Against Sewage, the Clean Water Sports Alliance, RSPB, The Women’s Institute, Angling Trust, SOS Whitstable, Wildlife and Countryside Link, The Rivers Trust, Ilkley Clean River Group, Soil Association and Windrush Against Sewage Pollution.
Marchers are encouraged to wear blue to symbolise clean water and to bring placards, puppets, posters, banners, costumes, marching bands and musical instruments.
The Environment Department was contacted for comment.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: I know the real reason Stonehenge was built – to ruin my holiday
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Labour has sunk plans to build a road under the ancient monument. It’s a blow to long-suffering drivers
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Rachel Reeves’ spending audit earlier this week proved that, if nothing else, she has excellent comic timing. With the school holidays upon us, a decent swathe of the population, my family included, is preparing for the summer mission to Cornwall. What could be more hilarious, in this context, than cancelling the Stonehenge tunnel?
The journey from the South East down to the ice-cream isthmus requires the kind of logistics and planning usually reserved for military invasions. Sure, the US Army could put a million men in the desert, but could they get a four-year-old and a toddler down to the first sunny weekend in Newquay?
As with missions to space, timing is everything. Miss your window and you might as well wait for the next favourable launch conditions, which could be the next day, or possibly the next year.
Everyone has their own advice for handling it. My mother, who favours the motorway route, even though the M4 takes you basically via Birmingham, says you “must” reach the M5 by 7am. She gives this advice with the foreboding of an ancient oracle. Nobody knows what happens if you don’t make the cut-off, but it can’t be good.
For the A303 lovers, the prospect of a tunnel has been a kernel of hope as you crawl through Wiltshire, something to think about as you Google which services have a McDonald’s and wonder who on earth stops to eat at those USA-style “diners” on the side of the road. We could daydream that one day we would no longer have to endure the whole “henge” situation. Instead we would zoom past it underground in a shiny new tunnel, thinking of Rick Stein and Poldark.
It was not to be. With one little word, “unaffordable”, the Chancellor condemned the A303 and the surrounding roads to be clogged like Brian May’s plughole for the rest of eternity.
Public opposition to the tunnel, led by the otherwise sensible historian Tom Holland, focused on the need to protect “our most sacred prehistoric landscape”. The essential mysteries about Stonehenge are the same as about Grant Shapps and Rita Ora: how did it get there, and why?
This week, we have our answer. Stonehenge was built by far-sighted West Country residents to inconvenience holidaymakers. Thousands of years ago, those canny druids were preparing to confound the second-homers, the down-from-towners, the Thule Legions.
It was ironic when Just Stop Oil painted Stonehenge orange just before the summer solstice: no inanimate object does more to discourage car use.
My daughter graduated this week. From nursery. When first I heard about this event I thought it sounded a bit silly: four-year-olds wearing mortar boards and gowns, celebrating heading off to reception. I was tempted to dismiss it as another unwelcome innovation from America, the nation of celebration inflation, which has given us endless “proms” and “sweet sixteenths” and other fripperies.
In fact the event was heart-melting. It is different when it is your own children. As our daughter and her classmates collected their scrolls and stood to sing the songs they had practised, there was hardly a dry eye in the playground. When your children are young you can convince yourself that you, too, are not really a parent. You alone have slipped the net, a young person who happens to have a child. Looking around, this illusion disintegrated. Here we were, unarguably mums and dads. A valuable lesson.
Besides, all the evidence tells us that the first few years are far and away the most important. Give me the child until nursery graduation and I will give you the woman, as Aristotle more or less said.
Getting through these first years intact is a more worthy moment of celebration than the 2.1 you scrape after three years getting sloshed and indebted in some provincial city.
The American table tennis player Lily Zhang was quoted in the papers this week expressing her bemusement that members of the public always think they could give her a game. It’s true that the Olympics lends itself to armchair rumination of this kind. With the right training, you think, pouring the second glass of cab sav, you too could be collecting your medal at rowing or cycling.
Table tennis is tempting because, unlike the 100 metres or the gymnastics, it doesn’t seem to require any outlandish physical gifts. I am not so deluded as to think I could win at ping pong, but the Turkish pistol shooter Yusuf Dikec, who has gone viral for being 51, wearing normal clothes and winning a silver medal in lackadaisical style, gives me hope. He says he is a ‘natural shooter’. Hope for us all.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/tv/0/the-las.title: The Last Leg’s Adam Hills: ‘There’s a whole gap in the Paralympics for people with my disability’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/tv/0/the-las.subtitle: Hills and his fellow hosts Josh Widdicombe and Alex Brooker are getting stuck in at the Paris Paralympics – and campaigning for a new sport
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/tv/0/the-las.text:
When Josh Widdicombe joined the pilot of comedy show The Last Leg – ­alongside host Adam Hills (born without a right foot) and sports journalist Alex Brooker (born with hand and arm abnormalities and a twisted right leg that was amputated when he was a baby) – he could have been forgiven for feeling some trepidation.
After all, on a panel described by Hills as “three guys with four legs”, he was the “token able-bodied sidekick” (so said a Channel 4 press release). But the 40-year-old insists that he had no sweaty palms. “Because I just thought it would be a late-night curio, I suppose. One of those shows where they say, ‘Tomorrow night, The Last Leg will be at the slightly later time of 1am’.”
That was back in 2012 when it was commissioned as a nightly round-up of Channel 4’s groundbreaking Paralympics coverage. It has since outlasted Clive James, the late doyen of TV critics (who said it was “almost the best part” of the “strong” Paras programming), the tenures of Nick Clegg, Jeremy Corbyn and John Bercow (who have all been guests) and the Iraq public inquiry. “Chilcot Inquiry,” Brooker said to guest Alastair Campbell in 2015 with one of his characteristic Mrs Merton-­­­style one liners. “On a scale of one to 10, how much are you s---ing ­yourself when that comes out?”
Moving from its now-regular weekly slot, it has returned to nightly instalments for the purposes of the Paris Paralympics. Shows continue to be live and guests from the games are plentiful.
When we speak shortly before the trio fly to France, Brooker is on a video call from his home in Huddersfield, with Hills joining from the National ­Tennis Centre in Roehampton, ­having spent the morning making social-media videos about accessibility (I catch up with Widdicombe a day later on a Zoom from his ­family holiday in Cornwall). Hills’s favourite event is the wheelchair basketball, which he says is “so graceful” it is almost balletic. Brooker prefers the brutality of wheelchair rugby: “It’s less ballet and probably more a mosh pit.”
But there is another sport that Hills wants to see added to the roster – para-standing tennis. “There’s a whole gap there for people with disabilities like me,” he says. “Because I don’t use a wheelchair.” He has made a documentary about his love of the sport for Sky and is lobbying for its inclusion. “We considered doing a bit of a Just Stop Oil and storming the courts in Paris and just playing our own game anyway. But we thought, let’s not get them offside so early on in the process.”
(Protestors from Just Stop Oil hijacked a live broadcast of The Last Leg in 2023.) Instead, the 54-year-old Australian is biding his time, hoping to compete at a home Paralympics in Brisbane in 2032. “That’s absolutely the dream,” he beams. “Look, I’ve got a pretty good doubles partner who reckons he can carry me even if I’m 62.”
Ant and Dec have suggested that this year’s I’m a Celebrity… jungle should be devoid of MPs after controversial appearances from Nigel Farage and Matt Hancock. But The Last Leg has entered the zeitgeist thanks in part to unforgettable cameos by politicians. ­Corbyn agreed to arrive in a limo and fur coat (“We’re still not entirely sure why his people said yes,” muses Hills). Ed Miliband mimed Take On Me by A-ha, before hanging around in the green room till 3am.
Meanwhile, a few days after Clegg’s interview – ­during which Brooker hit his “Bull-Button” nine times – the then-Lib Dem leader agreed to be Hills’s plus-one at a secret Prince gig. “We did stay in touch,” says Hills of the ­president of global affairs at Meta. “But now he’s in a way more powerful position than deputy prime ­minister.” “Yeah,” shouts Brooker. “He can access your Facebook!”
Since Channel 4 promoted its 2012 Paralympics coverage by ­putting billboards up after the Olympics closing ceremony declaring “Thanks for the warm-up”, the bold message of disability inclusion has spread across the TV landscape. In comedy, you have the likes of Rosie Jones (a former Last Leg researcher), Josh Pugh, Dan ­Tiernan, Lee Ridley and Chris McCausland. The latter is about to become the first blind contestant on Strictly Come Dancing, alongside deaf Love Island star Tasha Ghouri and three Olympians.
Despite the series being mired in scandal over allegations of abuse of celebrities by their professional partners, Hills says: “I think Strictly should be put up on a pedestal for what they’ve done. It’s that spoonful of sugar, isn’t it? It’s dancing, so you don’t realise that you’re receiving a lesson in disability awareness at the same time.”
Brooker, 40, says his sole talent contest ambition was achieved with an appearance as Bigfoot on ITV’s The Masked Singer in February. “I don’t want to roll the dice of trying to lift a professional dancer on television. The BBC don’t need that insurance risk.” “They’ve got enough going on!” Hills interjects, and both ­dissolve into giggles.
When I enquire whether either has actually been asked, Brooker chuckles again. “Oh, I’m going to say that laugh says Alex has been asked,” goads Hills. “Very rarely do I say this,” replies Brooker, who wears a prosthetic right leg, “but physically I don’t know if I could do it. But I would like to say, if Hills did Strictly, he would go very far. He would embrace the pain. And that’s a good thing about being disabled – our default position is one of slight uncomfortability. You know, when the doctors say to me, ‘What’s your pain threshold on a scale of one to 10?’ I say, ‘Well, I’m normally coasting at about four’.”
For his part, Hills fully accepts his raging competitive spirit. If he joined the show, he says: “There would be an inquiry into the way that the guest dancer was shouting at the professional.” The trio decline to take any credit for their impact on the public’s perceptions. But, just as the Bafta-nominated series can segue from the fluffiest of light entertainment to the weightiest of emotions – there was even a two-hour special on the anniversary of the murder of MP Jo Cox – Brooker suddenly shifts gears.
The former Press Association sports reporter looks back to 2012, the year that he started his career in television, and says of his personal transformation: “I can’t quantify it. It’s almost like I’ve had a form of therapy, sitting on the sofa, chatting about the things that I’m most self-conscious about. I’ve done it live on telly with Hillsy and Josh. And now the things that I used to see as negative, I celebrate.”
Yet perhaps the greatest indicator of the programme’s success is the desensitising of the audience to the hosts’ bodies. Brooker has said that people frequently forget he is actually disabled. Meanwhile, Widdicombe says that many viewers wrongly conclude he is. “Yeah, loads of them do. I think if you google ‘Josh Widdicombe’, ‘... disabled’ is one of the first things to come up. Which is annoying because it should be ‘... tour’.”
All three insist that they are shocked the show has lasted 12 years and 30 series (plus Christmas and elections specials). Hills now hopes that it can survive another eight years not just so he can compete Down Under at the Brisbane Games, but so the three of them can ignite the Olympic flame. Widdicombe belly laughs at the idea, before proposing a method one would have to call “The Lit Leg”.
“There’s no doubt about that – I’d say lighting Alex’s leg while it was still on, and him walking up there and kicking the leg off into the cauldron would be pretty impressive.” It certainly would. Only a fool should bet against it.
The Last Leg in Paris and Paris 2024 Paralympic Games is live on Channel 4 and YouTube until September 8

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Easy to be blasé when you’re disrupting other lives, judge tells Just Stop Oil activists
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Six protesters, five of whom are jailed, told that actions ‘were disproportionate to your aims’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
A judge sentencing Just Stop Oil protesters over an M25 demonstration told them that “it’s easy to be blasé” when it is other people’s lives they are disrupting.
Judge Shane Collery KC said “many people suffered hours of delay” and told the defendants: “Your actions were disproportionate to your aims.”
He said their purpose on Nov 9 2022 was to “create mass disruption so Just Stop Oil would benefit from the media interest it would create.”
The judge noted that an accident had happened near one gantry during the protest and it was “fortunate more accidents did not occur.”
He told Basildon Crown Court on Thursday that the defendants were all either retired, students or recent graduates at the time, saying: “It’s easy to be blasé and dismissive when it’s not your life that’s being disrupted.”
Judge Collery described the protest as “perhaps a curious way of seeking to influence the public opinion”.
He said the protesters considered they “knew better than everyone else”, and suggested an element may have been “the day out and perhaps the excitement of a day’s action”. He accepted the defendants were not the organisers of the protest, but said they were “willing volunteers”.
The judge said the court “accepts a conscientious motive may be a relevant consideration” but that the protesters’ actions were “disproportionate” to their aims.
He told the defendants: “You are all intelligent people and more than capable of working out why you’re in this position and what you need to do to avoid it.”
All the defendants pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing, as they were about to stand trial,  to causing a public nuisance.
The judge jailed George Simonson, 24, of Leeds, and 26-year-old Theresa Higginson of Biggleswade, Bedfordshire, for two years.
Simonsen smiled and waved to the public gallery as he was led to the cells, while Higginson shouted – referring to details heard earlier in the proceedings – that her “vegan diet did not make me ill”.
Paul Bell, 24, of Exeter, was jailed for one year and 10 months. He waved and blew kisses as he was led to the cells.
Gaie Delap, 77, of Bristol, and Paul Sousek, 73, of Bude, Cornwall, were jailed for one year and eight months. The judge told Delap: “Age, I regret, has not brought wisdom.”
Sousek said “thank you very much” after he was jailed, and tried to read from a document before he was bundled towards the cells by a security officer.
A sixth defendant, Daniel Johnson, 25, of Perth and Kinross in Scotland, was spared jail. The judge told him: “I’m prepared to accept the remorse expressed as genuine.”
He described Johnson as the “only defendant with a realistic prospect of rehabilitation” and sentenced him to 21 months in prison, suspended for 24 months, ordering that he complete 200 hours of unpaid work and pay £750 in costs.
The judge ordered that the activists’ climbing equipment, locks and banners be confiscated.
There had been gasps at the start of the judge’s sentencing when he told the six defendants: “In all but the case of Daniel Johnson, those [sentences] will be for immediate terms of imprisonment.”
The judge ordered that a second count of causing a public nuisance against all six should lie on the file.
Francesca Cociani, of Hodge, Jones & Allen, which represented Delap, Bell, Johnson, and Higginson, said: “Today’s decision to imprison peaceful protesters is a grave injustice and does not align with the UK’s professed values.
“Peaceful protest is a fundamental right and a vital tool for enacting positive societal change. Increasingly lengthy prison terms for these types of individuals were previously unseen, and it sends a disturbing message in our liberal democracy.
“We are exploring our options, including the possibility of an appeal, to challenge this decision and to defend the fundamental right to peaceful protest.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Watch: Chris Packham urges Barclays customers to set themselves on fire
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: BBC presenter criticised for ‘bizarre and outlandish’ comments during speech in Derbyshire
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
BBC presenter Chris Packham has been criticised after urging people who bank with Barclays to stick their heads in a bucket of petrol and set themselves on fire.
The 63-year-old Springwatch and Earth host made the comments at an Action for Wildlife Day event in Derbyshire.
The environmental campaigner urged people not to bank with financial institutions that invest in “fossil fuels, weapons and poverty”.
Speaking at the event last weekend at Carsington in the Derbyshire Dales, he said: “But, if anyone here is banking with Barclays, then, I suggest you stick your head in a bucket of fuel and set fire to it because you’re burning our planet down. And, it’s time to put this stuff behind us.”
His comments have been criticised as incitement, amid claims they are inappropriate for a leading BBC broadcaster.
Barclays declined to comment on Friday.
Tim Bonner, the chief executive of the Countryside Alliance, said: “It appears that in an increasingly desperate bid to stay in the media spotlight, Mr Packham is resorting to saying more and more bizarre and outlandish things to get noticed.
“Few are taking much notice, but it does pose serious questions for the RSPB, RSPCA and BBC about how much longer they can justify turning a blind eye to this behaviour, while allowing him to continue playing a significant role in representing them on the national stage and in family-friendly broadcasting.
“The respectability of all three organisations is on the line”.
A complaint about Packham’s comments was also made to Derbyshire Constabulary.
The complainant, a country sports enthusiast who wishes to remain anonymous, wrote to officers asking how the BBC presenter’s comments could be legal “given the recent spate of civil unrest which we have seen across the country” and those “inciting people to take direct action.”
A police spokesman said: “The video has been reviewed and no offences have been committed.
“Each incident that takes place is reviewed based on the language used as well as the specific set of circumstances in which the comments are made.
“In this instance, while there is legislation covering individuals encouraging or assisting a person or persons to cause serious harm to themselves, there is no suggestion that this is a serious attempt to influence anyone to commit any such acts.
“The words used in this instance do not reach the threshold for an offence and no action will be taken in relation to this incident.”
A BBC spokesman said: “Chris Packham is a freelancer, not a member of staff, and he’s not currently on air. His private activities and views are his own, not the BBC’s.”
Packham appeared at the event as the key speaker for Wild Justice, a pressure group that uses the legal system to try to get a better deal for UK wildlife by challenging government decisions through the courts.
Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion were also at the Action for Wildlife Day gathering, which was born out of an event called Hen Harrier Day.
For several years, Packham has been opposed to what he sees as the environmental damage and destruction of wildlife harrier habitats by the controlled burning of upland heather in a practice known as swaling.
Olivia Blake, the Labour MP for Sheffield Hallam, also appeared on stage at the event.
Last year, Packham stoked controversy after presenting a programme in which he questioned whether it was ethically acceptable to break the law in protesting against government climate policies.
Earlier this year, he told a court he “selectively” supports Just Stop Oil. He has also defended climate activists’ “right” to target MP’s homes as long as their actions were “peaceful and non-violent”.
Packham has not yet responded to a request for comment.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Can ‘two-tier Keir’ unite a fractured Britain?
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: With views on immigration dividing the nation, it falls to an ‘analogue leader in a digital world’ to offer the solution
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Are the riots over? It may still be too early to say, but if this week’s citizen-led fightback proves to have extinguished the flames, it will have done nothing to reassure the public that Sir Keir Starmer is the man who can prevent a repeat.
Critics say the Prime Minister has already alienated much of the country by “picking a side”. At a time when the nation so desperately needs someone who can bring people together, it instead has a leader who took the knee in 2020 even after the Black Lives Matter protests had turned violent.
Others have accused him of “hiding behind” the idea that the problem is confined to far-Right thugs rather than addressing issues that underlie some of the protests.
Growing numbers of MPs and peers of all stripes want the Government to acknowledge legitimate and deep-rooted societal problems, but Sir Keir has so far shown no sign that he is willing to do so.
On Thursday, Sir Keir visited a mosque in Solihull with Shabana Mahmood, the Justice Secretary, to give “necessary reassurance” to Muslims.
People living in white working-class communities – whose life chances are among the worst in the country – are now asking when Sir Keir will visit them to hear about their own concerns.
These are people such as Carol Lewis, 70, who has lived in the same house in Dagenham, East London, for her entire life and comes from a family that voted Labour for generations. She has now switched to Reform UK, saying: “The key issue for people here is immigration, of course it is.”
Lewis deplores the rioting, but says: “Starmer hasn’t acknowledged the real concerns of working people.” She believes that Sir Keir’s decision to be photographed taking the knee shows that “they will always pick a side, and they know which side they’re better off on. They know which side will vote for them. And it won’t be our side – the normal working class”.
Dagenham is typical of the “left behind” communities where tensions have been bubbling under the surface for years. One of the poorest boroughs in London, 29 per cent of its residents and 42 per cent of its children are living in poverty, according to the charity Trust for London.
Rob McNeil, the deputy director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, pointed out this week that asylum hotels are often located in deprived areas because they are cheaper for the government to rent out, which creates a sense of competition for resources between migrants and the poorest white people, both of whom are heavily dependent on the state for help.
Daniel Mansfield, a 41-year-old painter and decorator says that, in Dagenham, “People who’ve migrated here get priority on housing in this borough, I’ve felt that for years, and I’ve lived here my whole life.
“I’ve seen families being moved out and they’ve lost their property for it to be given to a family who’ve migrated here. The order of priority is a big thing.
“I don’t believe Starmer is the man to take us forward. I’d have kept the Conservatives or got Farage in.”
Figures released this week underscore the pressure on resources. They show that asylum seekers granted the right to stay in Britain now account for almost one in 10 of all homelessness claims. Under section 95 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, the Home Office can provide housing and financial support to a person who is seeking asylum and is destitute or is likely to become destitute within 14 days. After being granted asylum, migrants are required to find a place to live after 28 days – which many do by applying for help from councils.
Meanwhile, census data shows that, in terms of country of birth, 66.9 per cent of those born in the UK own their own home, falling to 37 per cent of those born in Africa. Conversely, 32.2 per cent of people born in Africa were likely to be living in social housing, the highest proportion of any group, compared with 16.9 per cent for those born in the UK.
Baroness Hoey, the former Labour home affairs minister, says Sir Keir must “stop trying to hide behind this idea that all of these problems have been caused by the far Right”.
She says that while there were clearly racists behind much of the violence, others are “people who are fed up and feel that no one is listening to them”.
She went on: “I don’t think he has grasped that, or if he has, he isn’t articulating that. Everything he has said is very one-sided; he doesn’t seem to show any empathy whatsoever with some of the reasons behind this.”
Polling supports her analysis. Just 31 per cent of Britons think he has handled the riots well, with Starmer’s description of rioters as “far Right” splitting the nation down the middle; only 52 per cent agree with that description. Most think the simple term “thugs” most appropriate.
In Hoey’s native Northern Ireland, where there has also been rioting in the past week, the issue of newly built flats being allocated to migrants rather than local people has been one of the causes of unrest, she says, coupled with images of hundreds of young men coming across the Channel illegally who are then housed by the taxpayer. Sir Keir, who has cancelled the Tories’ Rwanda plan, “hasn’t said anything about how they are going to stop people coming in every day”, she says.
Even if he did, would the public believe he had the interests of the whole country – including white people living in deprived areas – at heart?
Sir Keir likes to remind the public of his stint as Director of Public Prosecutions to show that he can be tough on crime, but his previous career as a human rights lawyer will also colour the public’s attitude on whether he can put his arms around those from both the Left and the Right.
This is, after all, a man who once asked “what role the police should play, if any, in civil society” when he was co-editor of a magazine called Socialist Alternatives in the 1980s.
Then, in 2019 he was anything but tough in his response to disruptive protests by Extinction Rebellion, saying that climate change was “the issue of our time and… the next generation [is] not going to forgive us if we don’t take action”. It is this failure to condemn disorder from some quarters that has led to a perception in some quarters of double standards, and earned him the nickname “two-tier Keir”.
When he was running for the Labour Party leadership in 2020, he promised to close immigration detention centres, and an article he had written in 1988 surfaced in which he said there was a “racist undercurrent” which “permeates all immigration law”.
Yet immigration is now ranked as one of the top three concerns for voters, according to the polling firm Ipsos, even as a separate poll by YouGov shows that Conservative voters and Labour voters are diverging in their views on migration for the first time in years – making it even harder for a Labour leader to bring the different political wings of the country together.
Sir Keir’s decision to be photographed taking the knee in support of the Black Lives Matter movement was a “disaster”, according to Lord Sewell, the author of a landmark report in 2021 on race and ethnic disparities. Meanwhile Baroness Hoey says: “I don’t remember him condemning some of the terrible violence there was with Black Lives Matter; it gave the impression that that seemed to be acceptable violence.
“He has got to remember, as Prime Minister, that he is not a lawyer acting for the European Court of Human Rights, and he needs to bring people together.”
Miriam Cates, the former Conservative MP, says that for successive elections the public has voted for lower immigration, and ended up with higher immigration, meaning “we’ve very much departed from democratic consent, and it’s the opposite of what people voted for when they got Brexit”.
She adds: “On the one hand, we say, well, we’re a democracy in this country. We sort our problems out democratically. But on this issue, democracy has clearly failed. What people have voted for consistently, the opposite has happened.”
Labour’s “loveless landslide”, with just 34 per cent of the vote in the general election, meant that the vast majority of people voted for parties that were promising to reduce migration.
Cates says: “[Sir Keir] can’t sort this out and appeal to both the people who are [protesting] on the streets and to his base… Nobody trusts him to sort this out, because the Labour Party’s record on immigration is one of liberal rules rather than cutting down, which is, of course, what the majority of people want.”
One ally of Sir Keir insisted that concerns about him taking the knee were overblown, saying: “One of Keir Starmer’s strengths has been his flexibility in going from a man who commanded support from a Corbynite Labour Party to a PM who beat a Right-wing Tory incumbent so convincingly.
“Prime Minister Starmer, who represents the necessary authority of the UK Government, is a different man than Keir the leader of the opposition who took the knee despite problems within the Black Lives Matter movement, and that’s a good thing.”
Migration, though, is not the only cause of unrest in the poor white communities where the rioting was most prevalent.
White British boys on free school meals in England lag behind almost every other ethnicity in Progress 8 attainment levels at secondary schools (the progress they make from the start of secondary school to their GCSEs). Only Irish Travellers and Roma gypsies do worse.
When it comes to social mobility, people of Chinese, Indian and Black Caribbean heritage have higher rates of long-term upward mobility than white British people, the Social Mobility Commission says.
According to the 2021 report of the Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities: “There is a sense of stagnation about the fate and life chances of poorer white groups, which is less the case with ethnic minority groups…
“Poor white groups, and especially poor white boys, do badly in the education system everywhere, whereas in some areas at least, especially London, poor ethnic minorities are improving rapidly.”
The true test of any leader is how they respond to events, and in Sir Keir’s case, the first big crisis he has faced has come less than four weeks into the job.
Some leaders rise to the challenge, like Volodymyr Zelensky, the president of Ukraine, finding resolve in abundance when they face the ultimate test. Others, like Sir Tony Blair, brilliantly make the most of a crisis, as he did when capturing the mood of the nation in his reaction to the death of Diana, Princess of Wales.
Then there are those whose weaknesses are horribly exposed by the first crisis they face, like George W Bush, who suffered mental paralysis when he was told about the 9/11 terrorist attacks, during his first year as president of the US.
Operationally, the Prime Minister has been accused of the plodding response of a lawyer when false rumours began to take hold about the Southport stabbings, rather than the fleet-footed reaction of a politician.
He has fretted over process rather than outcome, strapping himself into a straitjacket of correct procedure at a time when he needed to throw the rulebook out of the window.
Those with first-hand experience of previous political crises say that by failing to get the message out straightaway that the suspect in the Southport stabbings was neither an immigrant nor from a Muslim family, Sir Keir allowed disinformation to take root online, leading to the violence that has continued for more than a week.
In the days that followed the first of the riots, Sir Keir was accused of being too slow to convene the Cobra emergency committee, too slow to address the nation, dithering over whether to cancel his holiday, and too dismissive of the root causes of the trouble.
The King almost certainly would have spoken about the riots if No 10 had asked him to, but Sir Keir appears to have decided that he alone should speak directly to the country – yet he then waited until last Sunday, almost a week after the Southport incident.
He also took the unfathomable decision of engaging in a row with Elon Musk over so-called two-tier policing, committing the cardinal sin of dignifying the X owner’s comments with a response.
One former prime ministerial adviser says Sir Keir has proved to be “an analogue leader in a digital world”.
They say: “Right at the beginning, there was a huge missed opportunity to stop this. The information No 10 was getting from its social-media monitors would have shown them very quickly what people were saying about the Southport attack, and that was the moment to intervene.
“The police were refusing to say anything about the suspect, partly because he was under 18, and Sir Keir didn’t challenge that. But he could have said something, or told the police to say something, to debunk that false information circulating online. The consequences of not doing that have been severe.
“The law doesn’t necessarily help you when it comes to a crisis. Lawyers always want to tell you to say nothing, and they might win a case three years down the line, but by then huge damage might have been done by allowing a narrative to take hold unchallenged.
“Labour had a superb social media operation during the general election, and they should have been using those skills to promote things that were true to drown out those voices that are false, but they just didn’t.”
In Downing Street, Sir Keir had all the levers at his disposal to tackle the rioting, but appears to have fumbled when he reached for them. One former Cabinet minister says: “It seems to me that they were all asleep at the wheel. They lack operational nous and experience, because they are in-tray people.
“He should have been calling Cobra meetings straightaway, and even before that, the Home Secretary should have been going through the National Police Chiefs’ Council saying she wanted to speak to all of them to find out what was going on, but they failed to ask the right questions at the beginning.”
Sir Keir’s instinct as a lawyer was to turn to the courts to sort the problem out, and the swift justice and jail sentences meted out to rioters certainly had the public’s backing.
In the end, though, it was the public themselves who took matters into their own hands by gathering in their thousands to protect buildings targeted by rioters. Sir Keir could hardly claim credit for that, and it only added to the sense that he had failed to provide the solution.
John Reynolds, a 73-year-old retired tradesman in Dagenham, says: “Starmer doesn’t have the capability to sort this out, because he’s the cause.
“He doesn’t know what he’s doing and he’s the worst thing that’s ever happened to this country. He should be finding out what the problem really is rather than just responding with force.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: These sickening riots have exposed our social model as a fraudulent sham
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: None of Britain’s pathologies justify in any way the racist violence of recent days. The thugs must be defeated pitilessly
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Stop, just stop, all of you jabbering away on social media. Do not legitimise evil, wherever it comes from, and do not contextualise or rationalise any of the violence, the racism, the arson, the brick-throwing, the looting and the intimidation. Do not appeal to “root causes”; down that road lies relativistic hell. The rioters are atavistic barbarians, detestable nihilists; they have no excuses, no extenuating circumstances, no worthwhile message to convey. They must be caught and jailed, and the King’s peace re-established.
The vast majority, but not all, of the attacks on people and property in recent days have been led by far-Right fascists. The attack on a mosque in Southport was an anti-Muslim pogrom, a heinous act; the attempted burning of hotels containing immigrants was a depraved attempt at engineering a massacre. A Muslim-owned shop was incinerated in Northern Ireland, in a sickening echo of race riots past. There have been numerous racist attacks – white vandals hunting anybody looking non-white, and chanting slogans too grim to print. The targeting of immigration lawyers defiles the rule of law. The assaults against police, the destruction of property and the burning and looting of high street shops: the culprits are disgracing Britain.
The security in front of the mosque in my local area has been massively enhanced, with far more guards and stewards, all peering intently at the cars as they drive by. For the first time, a dog unit was parked in front. The fear and worry in that community at the surge in anti-Muslim hate in recent days is palpable. Members of other religious minorities are also on edge: imbecilic bigots have never been good at distinguishing between different non-Christian faiths.
Figures on the mainstream Right correctly refused to display any empathy towards the London rioters of 2011, or Just Stop Oil motorway saboteurs. It is dismaying, therefore, that some this time around fell into the trap of caveating their condemnation with references to the “understandable grievances” of the left-behind. The degenerates on our streets must be denounced out of hand, no ifs and no buts.
In this spirit, a second category of disgusting violence must also be called out: that being conducted by “sectarian gangs”, to use the terminology coined by Robert Jenrick, the candidate for Tory party leader. There has been a lot less of this violence than of the far-Right variety, but it deserves commensurate condemnation. This time, it has been the Left that has behaved hypocritically, seeking to downplay hatred.
Recent events in Birmingham were shocking. False rumours had circulated among the local Muslim community that far-Right agitators were about to descend, and counter-activists had gathered. An LBC reporter describes seeing hundreds of men, many “wearing hoods and masks, flying Palestinian flags and for some, carrying what appeared to be weapons”. The reporter was shouted at by passing cars, told that he “would regret” being in the area, ordered to leave and chased away by “six South Asian men [who] started walking towards us, carrying what looked like a metal pole”.
The police were not on the ground; he only saw “perhaps” two or three police cars drive by, without stopping, over a critical 40-minute period. A Sky News broadcast was interrupted by a masked man on a motorbike who sped up and shouted: “Yo, free Palestine, f--- the EDL”, and forced the reporters to depart. A man in a balaclava stabbed the tyre of one of Sky’s vans with a knife. A car was attacked, as was a pub, and a man injured.
Anti-white racism is as evil as any other kind of racism, and must be taken as seriously. The explanation from a police superintendent for the lack of police presence was problematic. He claimed the force’s response had been determined after meeting “community leaders”, helping it to “understand the style of policing we needed to deliver”. This two-tier approach cannot be the answer, and is undermining equality in front of the law.
I will highlight a third kind of violence this week: that of an Israelophobic or anti-Semitic nature. Some pro-Palestine activists, armed with axes and whips, ram-raided the UK HQ of an Israeli defence firm with a prison van and attacked staff and police with sledgehammers. The factory supplies technology to the British Army, and none of its output is used by the Israeli army (though it would be perfectly proper if it were). More generally, we have seen an explosion in far-Left and Islamist anti-Semitism since the October 7 attacks, and it is becoming normalised in an unforgivable display of double-standards.
All in all, Britain has a massive problem. Our model is a fraudulent sham. Our economy isn’t working, especially for the bottom end of the population. It isn’t working for entire regions. Our zero-sum game welfare state is crippled by massive dependency and a misplaced sense of entitlement.
We have been lulled into a false sense of complacency by the success stories of the British integration model – the collapse in racism, the surge in mixed marriages, the remarkable progress of many minorities in education, home ownership, income and politics, thanks to the legacy of the meritocratic and capitalist revolution of the 1980s and 1990s.
But this encouraged our centrist, “sensible” elites to turn a blind eye to the other side of the coin: the drastic decay and decline of opportunity in many provincial towns, juxtaposed with record immigration; the worrying prevalence of extremism, including anti-Semitism; increased ethnic conflict between minority groups; the election of sectarian MPs; and many other below-the-radar tensions.
We need a rethink on immigration, legal and illegal: we are incapable of integrating current volumes. Our long-standing approach to policing, with its proto-colonial emphasis on managing “community relations”, fetishises a failed kind of state multiculturalism. A colour-blind approach, centred on individuals not groups, is the solution.
We must reject woke identity politics: the far-Right is now adopting its grievance culture, seeking to radicalise elements of the white working class. Policing by consent is ending: we will need a lot more officers, as in France.
None of Britain’s pathologies justify in any way the racist violence of recent days. The thugs must be defeated pitilessly. This is time for moral clarity.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/us/news/2024.title: Hillary Clinton-run group helps fund Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/us/news/2024.subtitle: Onward Together set up by former presidential candidate to ‘defend our democracy’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/us/news/2024.text:
Just Stop Oil’s stunts are partly funded by a campaign organisation run by Hillary Clinton, US financial disclosures reveal.
A group founded by Mrs Clinton from the ashes of her failed presidential bid has donated $500,000 (£391,500) in the last three years to the protest group’s California-based financiers.
American voters who have bought tote bags decorated with pictures of Mrs Clinton or sweatshirts promoting abortion rights have inadvertently funded disruption in the UK.
Just Stop Oil’s largest financial backer is a controversial Californian non-profit, the Climate Emergency Fund (CEF), which pays for stunts by environmental groups across the world, including Extinction Rebellion.
A paper trail of transparency disclosures, seen by The Telegraph, shows that one of the CEF’s major supporters is Onward Together, a campaign organisation founded by Mrs Clinton in the aftermath of her 2016 presidential campaign against Donald Trump.
Onward Together gave $300,000 to the CEF in 2021, and a further $200,000 in 2022. The money donated by her group was placed into a fund that was used to pay for Just Stop Oil’s protests in the UK.
The donations are the largest contribution by Mrs Clinton’s organisation to a non-profit in the last three years, and are funded by public contributions and the sale of merchandise from her online shop.
However, although the Onward Together website lists a number of “partners” supported by her group, it makes no reference to the CEF or Just Stop Oil, who are the ultimate recipients of some of the money it has donated.
A separate arm of Onward Together contributes to specific candidates in US elections.
Organisations like Just Stop Oil are not required to disclose their funding in the UK, but the group has said it has received millions of pounds from the CEF, its largest supporter.
The group has previously been criticised for accepting money from foreign donors to fund its stunts, which have recently included the vandalism of Stonehenge and paint sprayed at Heathrow airport.
Some MPs have called for the group to be designated as a terror organisation. The total cost of policing Just Stop Oil by the Metropolitan Police alone was almost £20 million by the end of last year, and is now likely to be much higher.
The CEF was established in 2019 by Aileen Getty, the granddaughter of the oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, and campaigns for governments to adopt climate-friendly policies.
It is backed by several Hollywood celebrities, including Jeremy Strong, the Succession star, who sits on its board. Other major donors, other than Mrs Clinton, include a fund run by Susie Tompkins Buell, the co-founder of the North Face clothing brand.
Mrs Clinton’s support for the group, and indirectly for the protests of Just Stop Oil, is likely to come as a surprise to her own donors, who are told only that Onward Together is “committed to lifting up emerging organisations and leaders who are fighting for our shared progressive values and defending our democracy”.
Supporters can buy mugs and tote bags decorated with pictures of Mrs Clinton and the words: “Turns out she was right about everything.”
Other products include sweatshirts and baseball caps bearing the slogan: “Reproductive rights are human rights.”
Shoppers are told the proceeds contribute to “supporting progressive groups working to build a fairer, more inclusive America”, but there is no reference on the website to the CEF or its work funding disruption abroad.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: ‘My dad is a climate denier’: The Just Stop Oil poster girl who went from private school to prison
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Phoebe Plummer grew up in a loving middle-class family in Chelsea – now she’s facing prison, again. But how did it come to this?
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Growing up in a multimillion-pound Chelsea townhouse and afforded the finest private education, Phoebe Plummer knew nothing but privilege for the first 21 years of her life.
The star student made the most of it too, as a high achiever at her £50,000-a-year sixth form, St Mary’s School Ascot, and securing a place to study Computer Science at Manchester University. A comfortable life surely beckoned – perhaps, like her father and two older brothers, pursuing a lucrative career in insurance.
Yet, two years ago, a defining, headline-grabbing moment saw the promising student spurn her loving, middle-class background and settle on a decidedly different route in life – one of civil disobedience, handcuffs, and, ultimately, prison cells. On October 14, 2022, Ms Plummer made headlines across the world as she walked into the National Gallery and threw a tin of soup over Vincent Van Gogh’s masterpiece Sunflowers, worth an estimated £72.5 million, all in the name of climate justice.
The stunt, and her subsequent arrest, launched the pink-haired eco-warrior into the limelight – and set her on the path to becoming the “poster girl” for the controversial campaign group, Just Stop Oil (JSO).
The 22-year-old has since repeatedly broken her bail conditions to go on protest marches; she has attempted to confront MPs on their doorsteps, and, just this week, sprayed orange paint on departure boards at Heathrow Airport Terminal 5.
Given her generous upbringing, it is unsurprising that her transformation has not gone down well with her family. One of Ms Plummer’s brothers reportedly no longer talks to her, while her relationship with her father is said to be strained.
So how did it come to this? After St Mary’s School Ascot, whose alumni include the Duke of Kent’s grandchildren and the Princess of Monaco, Plummer joined Mander Portman Woodward College in Kensington, London, named “spoilt brat central” by Vice magazine in 2006, where she received top marks in her Chemistry, Computer Studies, and Maths A Levels. All was going well.
To those close to her, though, her change in direction was by no means a Damascene conversion. Ms Plummer – who identifies as queer and “non-binary but female-presenting” – had in her late teenage years increasingly embraced the counterculture. She went vegan, stopped flying, and stopped buying first-hand clothes. And, like many Gen Zers, she began to rally behind the climate cause, fearful of the existential risk it posed to her future, and was soon signing petitions, writing to MPs and joining marches.
With a London drawl, Ms Plummer is an eloquent and confident speaker, if a little blunt. (Readers may have watched her run-ins live on air with figures from former Conservative MP Jacob Rees Mogg to the BBC’s Victoria Derbyshire). She is well-versed in climate-speak, trotting out the same bitesize quotes in various interviews and rarely straying off topic. That is aside from one interview she gave in April last year to Tipping Points, a little-known podcast by a PHD student at Imperial College London.
Speaking with an ankle tag on, she gave a far more intimate take on why she felt it necessary to risk everything to become JSO’s agitator-in-chief. “It would be naive for me to turn around and say, ‘I have no worries about having a criminal record or having been to prison,’” she told the host. “It’s a big step to take. But for me, I had a flip in my brain where I thought all of these plans and hopes and aspirations I have for my future, for a career, for a family. They don’t exist unless I fight for a future in which they’re possible.”
“Right now, the only future I see for myself is one of mass famine and constant drought, of wildfires and floods, and societal collapse. There’s no career on that kind of planet. There’s no having a family on that planet. So direct action is the best way I can secure my future – not with a university degree as it should be.”
Ms Plummer’s first short stint in prison was in November 2022, when she should have been enjoying her Fresher’s term at The School of Oriental and African Studies in London after dropping out of Manchester. Instead, she was sent to HMP Bronzefield on remand after breaking bail conditions. A fortnight after the Van Gogh arrest, she joined dozens of other JSO protestors in blocking the M25, causing four-days of travel chaos.
Though intended as a punishment, Ms Plummer told the podcast that enduring Europe’s biggest female prison – whose 540 inmates reportedly include Lucy Letby – was in fact “very doable, very manageable”. Lying in the shadow of Heathrow airport, the privately-run jail is said to be one of the nicer places in the UK to be incarcerated, with the amount spent per prisoner £10,000 higher than at any other comparable facility in the country. It was reportedly the first in the UK to have its own branch of the Women’s Institute, which provides prisoners with resettlement programmes prior to their release. Inspectors in a recent report praised the “impressive array” of activities on offer for prisoners, which include Zumba and “legs, bums, and tums” classes.
During Ms Plummer’s first spell, nearly two dozen inmates staged a production of West End musical Betty Blue Eyes that was “deemed a great success”. Allowed to share a cell with a fellow JSO activist, and regularly seeing others who had taken action over the M25, she said: “It was nice in prison because there’s the space and the time to have the conversations about why you’re there.” Ms Plummer – who said her greatest heroes the Suffragettes had also faced jail in their fight for social change – added: “I think my biggest power in there was knowing I was in there for the right reasons.”
The impact on her family, however, was not quite so easy. “My family have struggled to deal with it,” she told the podcast. “One of my brothers told me I wasn’t his sister anymore, and that he wanted nothing more to do with me, and that he was ‘beyond disgusted’ and ashamed by me. And that’s harder, I can’t pretend that it’s not.” She told the host how, after her brother got engaged and spoke about wanting to start a family, she told her mother: “When they have children, I will feel more grief than joy.” This reaction was, she said, because she was “so scared about the world that their child would grow up in”.
Conversations with her father, meanwhile, have been painful. “My dad is a climate denier,” she said, “which makes it very hard to even start having the conversations about why I do what I do”. Though initially causing her deep anger, they have tried to find common ground and rebuild their relationship, connecting “more on an emotional level, about why I’m so scared, so outraged a lot of the time, than on a pure scientific basis”.
“I’ve come to a level of understanding that I’m asking them to deal with something pretty big – to accept the fact that I’ve gone to prison. It’s not something they ever thought their child would do,” she added.
Since then, Ms Plummer – who was recently registered in court as living in a large house in Clapham, south London, on a street where houses cost upwards of £4 million – has only upped the ante, having been arrested several more times for breaching bail conditions. She has further embraced her rock star image, posing last summer as Mona Lisa for an arty feature in fashion magazine Dazed. With “STOP OIL” emblazoned across her chest and holding a can of Heinz tomato soup, she wore a silk and cotton sweater by the exclusive Italian brand Loro Piana, whose jumpers can cost upwards of £1,000.
Last week, Ms Plummer and fellow activist Anna Holland, both 22, were both found guilty of criminal damage over the Van Gogh incident. With sentencing due in late September, Southwark Crown Court Judge Christopher Hehir warned them both to be “prepared in practical and emotional terms to go to prison”. And given his words came just days after five other Just Stop Oil protestors received record multi-year jail terms for conspiring to block the M25, it may be for some time.
In a recent interview, however, she addressed her privilege and the criticism JSO has received, including accusations that its ranks are filled by “posh” members who disrupt the lives of those less well-off with their abrasive tactics. “I don’t have to work three jobs to feed my kids or pay heating bills,” Ms Plummer told The Times, “which means I can dedicate time towards fighting for the people that don’t have the means to fight right now and are being hit hardest”. Soon, she may not even have that luxury.
The Telegraph contacted Ms Plummer for comment, but was told by JSO that she was unable to respond as she was currently “in prison”.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: Ed Miliband is putting Britain’s future in the hands of eco-fanatics
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: No one voted for anti-growth, anti-capitalist green groups to use lawfare to control our economic fate
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
Perhaps Greta Thunberg could be put in charge of the Bank of England. Caroline Lucas could be appointed to oversee the Treasury. A couple of activists from Just Stop Oil could be let out of jail to run the Department of Business and Trade, while some from Extinction Rebellion could take over at the Office for Budget Responsibility.
It may sound like a parody. And yet, Ed Miliband, the Energy Security and Net Zero Secretary, has just effectively given Greenpeace control over elements of our energy policy. And we are well on the way to handing anti-growth, far-Left eco-activists far too much influence over our economic fate.
The trouble is, no one voted for that. And even worse, it will end up impoverishing us all.
The North Sea had already become a hostile legal and regulatory environment for anyone still brave enough to try and make a living from exploring for oil and gas and delivering it to British homes and businesses, to keep the lights switched on and the heating running through the winter.
They already face bans on expanding their business, and punitive windfall taxes in the event that they ever manage to make a profit. Many of them have quite sensibly already decided enough is enough and pulled out, preferring to put their money to work somewhere else or simply to do nothing instead.
And yet, they face full-scale lawfare as well.
Miliband decided that his department would not fight a climate lawsuit challenging licences granted to the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields, two of the largest potential developments left in the region. He argues that it would save the taxpayer money.
It will no longer contest the challenges brought against them by Greenpeace, and its fellow climate campaign group, Uplift. And while it will be up to the courts to make the final decision, the licences look as good as finished. The slow death of the North Sea has now taken another decisive step forwards.
This is crazy. There are three big flaws with this decision.
To start with, when did Miliband’s department last display any interest in saving taxpayer money? GB Energy, the new, £8.3bn, state-owned company has been on a hiring spree. But no one yet seems to have a clear idea what it will actually do.
If Miliband is suddenly so worried about how taxpayer money is being spent, then perhaps he should start there – instead of pinching a few pennies on the legal fees for contesting this legal action.
After all, at least Rosebank and Jackdaw would, if allowed to go ahead, definitely generate some actual energy. This is more than can be said for the Government’s odd investment vehicle.
Next, the door has been opened for green activists to use lawfare to control our economic fate. With this decision, any green pressure group may be tempted to launch a judicial review. And if the Government won’t oppose it, then they have a veto.
Some of these organisations are well-meaning and interested in steadily reducing carbon emissions, improving air quality and protecting biodiversity. Others are not. Among them are anti-growth, anti-capitalist groups, committed to radically changing the way we all live and work.
Extinction Rebellion argues for citizen assemblies to control society – not just against climate change. Others support wealth taxes, unlimited immigration and a far-reaching retribution of power. Its agenda goes far beyond reducing carbon emissions.
Finally, who exactly voted for this? In the election earlier this year, Greenpeace ranked the Green Party as the most closely aligned with its values and beliefs and the Liberal Democrats as the next closest. And yet, those were the two parties that came fourth and fifth in the total number of votes cast.
Ministers ought to represent the voters who supported them – and preferably the wider electorate as well.
There are already environmental protests against the Government’s decision to increase the number of flights permitted from London’s City airport. Is that going to be stopped as well? What of Miliband’s plans for onshore wind farms or Angela Rayner’s plans for new towns and more housebuilding? The list goes on.
Handing too much power and influence to pressure groups – especially when they represent such a tiny section of the electorate – would be irresponsible and would hinder any government from implementing the manifesto on which it was elected.
Environmental campaigners trying to stop any further development of the North Sea are of course entitled to their views. They can bring legal action if they believe they have a case and if their supporters are willing to pay for it.
But they should not be allowed to operate as back-seat drivers, playing a role in how the British economy is run. The blunt truth is that the UK will need North Sea oil and gas for many years to come even as we steadily transition to a carbon-neutral economy. It is cheaper and more reliable to develop our own energy instead of relying on imports.
You would think the minister in charge of energy policy would be able to see that.
