https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Thugs rioted because they thought they could get away with it – it’s that simple
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: The vital takeaway from the past two weeks is that robust policing and stiff sentencing are the way to uphold public order
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Only now, as they appear at court, do we see what manner of men they are. Derek Drummond, the first rioter to be sentenced, was jailed for three years after punching a policeman during the unrest in Southport. He had 14 previous convictions from 19 offences, including for violence.
Drummond was in no sense untypical. Look at the other rioters appearing before Liverpool Crown Court. While some had clean sheets, many had what the police call “previous”. John O’Malley had a conviction for battery, while Declan Geiran had 13 convictions for 18 offences, including breach of a community order and malicious communications. Adam Wharton had 16 convictions for 26 offences, including robbery and burglary.
You get the picture.
These are not patriots driven to breaking point. They are not activists at all. Several are habitual criminals who have long preyed upon the people around them, and who spotted an opportunity in the chaos.
When dramatic things happen, commentators tend to look for commensurately dramatic explanations. Are we seeing the result of poverty and neglect? Does it have to do with mass immigration? Is it caused by Russian dezinformatsiya amplified by social media?
Possibly. Then again, on the principle of Occam’s Razor, we should look for the simplest explanation, the explanation that requires the fewest assumptions. And the simplest explanation here is that these ruffians thought they would get away with it.
They knew that political activists are rarely treated as common criminals. They had seen vandalism indulged when it was carried out in the name of BLM, Just Stop Oil or anti-Israel marches, in a way that it never is from, say, football hooligans.
More to the point, they had heard the new government loudly and performatively declaring that Britain’s prisons were full. How clever that announcement must have seemed at the time, using the post-election honeymoon to prepare the ground for less incarceration while blaming the Tories. It doesn’t look so clever now, though, does it?
One of the most depressing aspects of the past week has been the readiness of people who ought to know better to, if not exactly justify the violence, at least contextualise or rationalise it. “Of course I condemn lawlessness, but we need to understand people’s concerns about immigration…”
No. There is no excuse for attacking police officers. There is no excuse for setting fire to buildings. Such behaviour would be appalling at any time, let alone after the horrible murders in Southport, which should have brought the nation together in sympathy rather than dividing it in acrimony.
Rationalisation, though, is the stock-in-trade of the political commentator. Cast your mind back to the 2011 riots, which followed the shooting by a police officer of a black man named Mark Duggan. Then, as now, pundits and politicians lost no time in explaining to the rest of us what it was really about.
Some said poverty, others family breakdown, yet others police racism. Funnily enough, everyone seemed to have an explanation that chimed with their previous assumptions. Ken Livingstone blamed government cuts. Cristina Odone blamed absent fathers. David Lammy blamed a breakdown between police and ethnic minorities. David Starkey blamed gang culture.
Perhaps some of these things were contributing factors. But, again, Occam’s Razor suggests something more straightforward. When a vigil for Duggan in Tottenham turned violent, the police, whether because they were outnumbered or because they feared being accused of racism, looked on passively. Television images were broadcast around the country, telling every potential looter that the police had lost their nerve. The following night, riots and robberies spread across London. The day after, other English cities followed suit.
Not every news event slots into some sociological meta-narrative. Sometimes, the obvious explanation is the right one. If there are plenty of coppers about, if those coppers apply the law rigorously, and if property crimes and disorder are punished, people behave better.
One Labour MP who got it right was the policing minister, Dame Diana Johnson. Asked by the BBC on Thursday morning why there had been no violence the previous night, she replied that severe sentencing had an obvious deterrent effect, and that “the police were out in large numbers”.
For what it’s worth, I am not sure there was ever going to be trouble on Wednesday. The extreme Right in this country is small, disorganised and dim, and reports of planned anti-immigrant gatherings seem to have originated from a single message on Telegram.
Perhaps it was a genuine attempt by the far-Right to make trouble. Perhaps it was a false flag operation intended to galvanise the other side. Or perhaps it was a random message by a lone loser.
Whatever the explanation, counter-demonstrators found themselves with no one to demonstrate against.
Still, Dame Diana’s point stands. If you want to uphold public order, make sure the police are visible and that malefactors get stiff sentences. The unrest has allowed Labour ministers to be tough on crime while feeling good about it, because they see themselves, in Sir Keir Starmer’s words, “protecting communities” from “the far-Right”. That is indeed part of their job. But so is protecting “communities” (Labour’s collectivist codeword for ethnic minorities) from ordinary criminals. Indeed, as we are seeing in the courts, those two things are closer than Starmer allows.
It won’t do to maintain, on the one hand, that prison doesn’t work, while claiming, on the other, that the only way to deal with racist hooligans is a stiff jail term. If prison is the way to deal with racist hooligans – and it is – then it must also be the way to deal with other hooligans, whatever their beliefs.
Consider, for example, the serious violence directed against the police in June 2020, which saw 22 officers injured over two days in London. On that occasion, instead of demanding prison sentences, Starmer sank to one knee in sympathy with the perpetrators. BLM violence, in his mind, is evidently not the same as anti-immigration violence.
The same double standard may explain why he talks exclusively of the far-Right, mentioning neither the answering Muslim gangs nor unpolitical violence of the kind we have just seen in Southend, where gangs fought with machetes.
But criminals are criminals, regardless of motive. BLM violence is not justified by anti-racist ideology. Islamist terrorism is not justified by hostility to Western foreign policy. Far-Right violence is not justified by concerns about immigration. Offenders should be dealt with disinterestedly, uniformly and predictably.
In an open society, we should be free to debate the causes of disorder as loudly as we wish. Provided we stop short of incitement, we should be allowed to say whatever we want about immigration, race or religion. Starmer’s threats against online platforms are authoritarian and counterproductive.
But decent people should never use criminals as props in their arguments. Politicians do it far too often: “There will be a return to violence if there is border infrastructure in Ireland”; “We bring this on ourselves by going along with Israel”; “Immigration makes tensions inevitable”.
By all means debate these things. My own view is that high levels of immigration, unless accompanied by vigorous cultural assimilation, reduce the social capital that homogenous societies enjoy. But that argument is a world away from the numbskulls who, in response to the heartbreaking deaths of little children, went on a spree of looting and arson.
Anti-immigration protesters, Hamas sympathisers, eco-activists, ordinary criminals. It should make no difference. Governments are there to protect life, liberty and property. If that means building more prisons, ministers should get on with it.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Just Stop Oil claims climate change will lead to Southport-style riots
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: The group warns that violence and disorder could follow if the Government does not move to ban fossil fuels
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Just Stop Oil has claimed climate change will lead to Southport-style riots in the future after police arrested four of its members who were on their way to protest at Manchester Airport.
Greater Manchester Police said it had detained three women aged 21, 30 and 53 and a man aged 23, on Monday morning, on suspicion of conspiring to cause a public nuisance.
In response to the arrests, a spokesman for Just Stop Oil said the violent riots currently taking place across the UK “are a foretaste” of what would happen if the group’s demands are not met.
Just Stop Oil is calling on the Government to establish a “fossil fuel treaty” banning all use of oil.
It vowed in July to use “all means necessary” to disrupt families’ summer holidays to draw attention to its demands.
A spokesman said on Monday: “The rioting and racist attacks that have occurred over the weekend are a foretaste of what will come as climate breakdown progresses and puts unbearable pressures on society. The root causes of these riots are clear.
“Austerity; manipulative far-right agitators in the streets, the media, and in Parliament; and the liberals that fail to challenge their agenda. Imagine when food scarcity, home-destroying floods, and global collapse are mixed in?”
Riots continued across Britain on Sunday as groups of Muslims clashed with far-Right rioters who were setting fire to accommodation used to house asylum seekers.
Hotels were set on fire in Rotherham and Tamworth, while in Bolton, rival groups of anti-immigrant and Muslim youths were kept apart by police.
The violence follows widespread disorder across the country on Saturday which saw riots taking place in Belfast, Nottingham, Liverpool, Stoke and Hull.
In an emergency address from Downing Street, Sir Keir Starmer warned the rioters would regret taking part and vowed to do “whatever it takes to bring these thugs to justice as quickly as possible.”
The latest Just Stop Oil arrests come after a series of damp squib protests at London Heathrow airport last week – and mark the group’s first attempt to target Manchester, the UK’s second-largest airport.
Chief Superintendent Mark Dexter, Greater Manchester Police’s head of specialist operations, said: “We have been working hard with colleagues from Manchester Airport and police forces across the country, sharing intelligence, with the common goal to prevent these disruptive and targeted attacks on our airports.
“These arrests have no doubt prevented a determined and targeted attack which would have brought significant delays and upset to those hard-working people heading off for their summer holidays.”
The four remain in police custody and the force said its inquiries are ongoing.
Several of the group’s activists sat or stood by the gates to departures in Heathrow Terminal Five on Thursday before some were physically removed by the police.
The group claimed a total of 17 people had been arrested on Thursday morning, including 10 detained on public transport, six who were blocking travellers inside the terminal building and one person who was said to be filming the protesters.
Just Stop Oil regularly publishes its own pictures and videos on social media in an attempt to drum up public support for its disruptive protests.
A week ago holidaymakers at Gatwick Airport were forced to step over activists who had attempted to block security gates, while on Tuesday two Just Stop Oil members reportedly sprayed information boards, windows and the floor at Heathrow Terminal Five’s departures area with orange paint.
One of last week’s Heathrow protesters, 22-year-old Phoebe Plummer, was out on bail after being found guilty of vandalising Vincent Van Gogh’s painting Sunflowers in 2022 by throwing a tin of tomato soup over it.
She has since been remanded in custody.
Manchester Airport declined to comment on Monday morning’s arrests, saying they were a police matter.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: It’s not all fake news on Twitter that Musk’s critics would ban. It’s fake news they don’t like
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: NHS privatisation fantasies, BLM riot incitement, made-up Gammon stories – those are all fine
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
For well over a decade, Twitter (or “X”, if you absolutely insist) was the go-to online platform for Britain’s opinion-forming classes. Under its new management by the contrarian tech billionaire Elon Musk, they are rapidly falling out of love with it.
In recent days, a number of high-profile progressive journalists and activists have called for major restrictions on the use of the platform, or even for it to be shut down altogether. They blame Twitter for misinformation that was circulating in the wake of the Southport stabbings, and they blame that misinformation for the far-right riots that subsequently erupted.
Their evidence for this is rather flimsy. It is true that speculation about the killer’s identity – more specifically, the false claim that he was a Muslim asylum seeker – spread initially via Twitter. However, when it was revealed two days later that the suspect was neither a Muslim nor a refugee, but a British-born son of immigrants from the predominantly Christian country of Rwanda, this information spread just as rapidly – also, in part, via Twitter. It did nothing to curb the riots.
Far-right racists, it turned out, are not that discerning. They are not going to say “If the perpetrator was a Muslim who arrived via the asylum route, I’ll do some rioting; however, if the suspect was of Rwandan Christian heritage, then that obviously changes everything. In that case, there’s no way I’ll riot.”
That is not how these people roll.
Fair enough, a Twitter critic might say, maybe these riots would have happened anyway, with or without Twitter. But is misinformation not a general problem that needs to be regulated? Even if it does not lead to identifiable harmful outcomes?
Speaking as a seasoned Twitter keyboard warrior, my impression is that “misinformation” and “fake news” are largely demand-driven. It is not that people fall for sophisticated hoaxes, which only a professional fact-checker could identify as such. Rather, social media users fall for very obvious hoaxes when they appear to confirm their prejudices. They fall for them because they want to fall for them.
Take “RS Archer”, a very obvious fantasy figure, who pretends to live in a mansion in France, in great style and luxury. He constantly tells implausible anecdotes about implausibly clichéd, implausibly stupid British “Gammon” types that he allegedly comes across, because his audience is the sort of Brit who likes to feel intellectually and culturally superior to “typical” Brits. RS Archer has close to 125,000 followers.
Or take Dr Julia Grace Patterson, who, unlike RS Archer, is at least a real person, but who campaigns against something which is demonstrably not real: the privatisation of the NHS. She has over 270,000 followers, who eagerly lap up her conspiracy theories.
Misinformation merchants of that variety do not cause much harm. They simply tell their audience what they want to hear, and then enjoy the attention and the adoration they get in return. But the point remains that Twitter has always been rife with varying degrees of “misinformation”. And sometimes, it does have consequences.
The not-always-peaceful Black Lives Matter protests were massively amplified by Twitter, as are the Palestine marches today, or the actions of militant eco-socialist groups such as Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. I do not remember anyone calling for a clampdown on Twitter in that context.
I am not saying that left-wing progressives are more prone to spreading, or consuming, misinformation than people elsewhere on the political spectrum. But since British political Twitter is a predominantly left-wing, progressive platform, in absolute terms, most misinformation comes from the progressive Left.
It is not really “misinformation” as such that bothers Twitter’s newfound progressive critics. It is the fact that they are no longer quite as hegemonic on that platform as they once were. It is the competition they don’t like, and as incumbents often do, they are now calling for regulation to protect their market-dominant position.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/books/non-fi.title: Soviet dissidents? Funnier than you might think
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/books/non-fi.subtitle: Benjamin Nathans’s To the Success of Our Hopeless Cause examines the bravery – and weary wit – of those who took on the USSR from within
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/books/non-fi.text:
The pro-democracy protest of the Russian teenager Olga Misik went viral in 2019. Powerful images showed a 17-year-old sitting cross-legged in front of armed riot police in ­Moscow and reading to them from the Russian constitution. With stubborn calm, she insisted on the principles they were supposed to uphold: the right to protest and freedom of speech.
Olga wasn’t trying to bring down the system. She was holding it to account, demanding the authorities abide by their own rules. In the eyes of the West, this may seem counter-intuitive. Our protest movements lean on traditions of civil disobedience, public acts of breaking the law. Think of Rosa Parks’s violation of segregation laws in Alabama, the illegal tactics of the suffragettes or the vandalism of Just Stop Oil.
In Russia, however, civil obedience has long roots. It is a tactic explicitly formulated and pioneered by the poet and mathematician Alexander Esenin-Volpin (1924-2016) in the post-Stalin era. As an unkempt eccentric who roamed the streets of Moscow in his house ­slippers, he was hardly the stuff of heroic legend. But his insistence that everyone should observe the written law of the Soviet Union to the letter caught on, creating a distinct movement whose legacy lives on today.
A new book by Benjamin Nathans, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania, sets out to deliver the definitive history of dissent in the USSR, from famous, Nobel Prize-winning dissidents such as the physicist Andrei Sakharov (father of the Soviet hydro­gen bomb) and the novelist Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (author of The Gulag Archipelago) to less well-known figures. To the Success of Our Hopeless Cause offers refreshingly clear-eyed insights into the idiosyncratic world of those who fought for freedom behind the Iron Curtain.
The struggle wasn’t quite as hopeless as the book title suggests. It’s borrowed from the movement’s favourite drinking toast and speaks volumes about its habitual, gentle self-mocking. The Dutch writer Karel van het Reve, an ally of Soviet dissidents who helped disseminate their writings abroad, once received a certificate from them that declared him “an honourable and indispensable participant in all protests” and demanded that “this document is to be presented to organs of the police, procuracy, and the KGB”.
Not taking themselves too seriously is one of many distinguishing features of Soviet dissidents, highlighting the need to understand them within the world that made them. As Nathans reminds us, Western observers “were quick to cast the contrarians as surrogate soldiers of Western liberalism”, when in fact they were nothing of the sort. Of course they interacted with liberal democracies, not least because this always provoked a response, but they were Soviet people. Looking at the West, many had “misgivings about multi-party democracy, rampant consumerism, and perceived lack of firmness in confronting the Kremlin”.
They never wanted to destroy the Soviet Union. After all, the constitution of the USSR enshrined freedom of speech and assembly. The problem was that nobody took that seriously, neither the regime nor the majority of citizens, who had learnt to circumvent the system. Nobody stuck to the law and everyone knew it. As one dissident put it, “because of their way of life, the overwhelming majority of citizens in a communist society feel no need for civil liberties. And precisely for this reason they don’t have those liberties.”
The Soviet Union was like a great play in which everyone knew their lines. Some of the cast believed the story, most played along in exchange for a relatively quiet life – a strategy that worked for many once Stalinist terror had given way to a less murderous form of socialism.
Soviet dissent never managed to bring the house down, nor did it seek to do so – a pattern with parallels in Russia today. But it “broke the fourth wall”, as Nathans puts it. It spoke to the audience, corroding the collective charade. The effects of this were obscured by the ­continuous lip service most paid the system right to the end, but they help explain the lack of resistance to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. Few were sorry when the curtain fell.
To the Success of Our Hopeless Cause empathetically traces the ­stories of those who broke the rules by sticking to the law. The book’s dense academic style and vast scope don’t make for light fare – it can be tough going, keeping track of a flurry of names and details all building on one another across its 800 pages. Yet readers who stick with it are rewarded with a host of original insights, shedding light on a remarkable cast of individuals who never succumbed to political apathy at a time when most did.
Katja Hoyer’s latest book is Beyond the Wall: East Germany, 1949-1990. To the Success of Our Hopeless Cause is published by Princeton for £35. To order your copy for £30, call 0808 196 6794 or visit Telegraph Books

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/cricket/2024.title: MCC churn continues as chief executive leaves post to run Cheltenham racecourse
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/cricket/2024.subtitle: Guy Lavender steered the club through Covid in a strong financial position and oversaw the redevelopment of Lord’s
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/cricket/2024.text:
The changing of the guard at Lord’s will continue when Guy Lavender leaves his post as MCC chief executive this year.
Lavender has landed a job in charge at Cheltenham racecourse, and will leave MCC at the turn of the year.
He joined MCC in October 2017 from Somerset, where he was also chief executive. Before moving into sports administration, he had an 18-year career in the Parachute Regiment, retiring as a lieutenant colonel in 2006.
The 57-year-old’s departure continues the churn at the top of MCC. In October, Mark Nicholas will move from the role of president to chairman, replacing Bruce Carnegie-Brown, who did not seek re-election for a second term. Mervyn King, the former governor of the Bank of England, will take over as president for 12 months.
In addition, Jamie Cox left to become Somerset chief executive, with Rob Lynch, the former chief executive of the Professional Cricketers’ Association, joining to replace him in the role of director of cricket and operations.
Lavender has been a steady hand during a tumultuous period in the club’s history in which relations with pockets of the membership have, at times, been tense.
The club attempted to move “historic fixtures” such as Eton v Harrow and Oxford v Cambridge away from Lord’s, but was met with resistance from members. The fixtures are still played at the ground, despite a recommendation from last year’s Independent Commission for Equity in Cricket report stating that they should be moved.
Lavender has also had to manage the fallout of comments made by his colleagues. Carnegie-Brown was caught in a hot-mic incident at the club’s AGM in 2022. Believing his microphone was off towards the end of a break in the meeting, Carnegie-Brown said “I expect they are taking an age to empty their colostomy bags”. Stephen Fry, the former president, has also infuriated sections of the membership with comments about the club.
Last summer, Lavender had to address members in the Long Room after the Australian team alleged they were physically and verbally abused on their walk back to the changing room following the controversial stumping of Jonny Bairstow towards the end of a heated Ashes Test that had earlier seen England wicketkeeper Bairstow pick up a Just Stop Oil protester and remove him from the pitch. One member was expelled from the club and two more were handed long suspensions for their part in the Long Room fracas.
Lavender steered the club through Covid in a strong financial position and has overseen the various stages of the redevelopment of Lord’s, including the rebuilding of the Compton and Edrich Stands at the Nursery End, which began in 2019. Work will begin later this year on the redevelopment of the Tavern and Allen Stands.
The last few months of Lavender’s premiership are crucial for the club’s future, too. The MCC, as one of the owners of the eight host venues, is set to be handed a 51 per cent stake in a team in the Hundred by the England and Wales Cricket Board.
In the case of Lord’s, this means 51 per cent of London Spirit. The ECB will sell 49 per cent of Spirit to private investors. The MCC, as host, has the right of veto over its partners, and can choose to sell some, none or all of its share.
The MCC has sought to work collaboratively with its 23,000 members over this issue. In that spirit, it will host a special general meeting over the next two months to vote on whether to accept the ECB’s gift.
The MCC has already begun a formal process to replace Lavender, led by the nominations committee. Nicholas, who has a three-year term as chairman, is likely to have a say and the prestige of the role will attract interest from across the globe, and from within and outside the game.
Nicholas, the former Hampshire captain and veteran broadcaster, has already stamped his mark on the club as president. He led the inaugural World Cricket Connects, a conference of some of the game’s leading figures last month. Nicholas said in June that he wants to make the club “fun” again, and cited membership harmony as his first priority.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Just Stop Oil Heathrow airport protest fails – again
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Demonstration follows several other attempts to block holidaymakers at airports this week
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters have been removed from Heathrow airport following another failed protest.
Several activists sat or stood by the gates to departures in Terminal Five before some were physically removed by police.
It followed several other damp squib demonstrations at airports this week.
On Monday, holidaymakers at Gatwick stepped over activists who had attempted to block security gates, while on Tuesday two Just Stop Oil members reportedly sprayed information boards, windows and the floor at Heathrow Terminal Five’s departures area with orange paint.
A Heathrow spokesman said: “Earlier this morning, a protest incident in Terminal Five was swiftly resolved, and all involved were immediately removed from the airport.
“Our priority will always be to maintain the safety of passengers and colleagues, and we’ll continue to work closely with our partners and the police in taking proportionate action to protect travel plans this summer. Unlawful and irresponsible protest activity is not the way forward, and will not be tolerated.”
The Telegraph understands that Thursday’s Heathrow protesters did not daub orange paint on anything and did not glue themselves to the floor or any other structures.
Just Stop Oil, which is calling on the Government to establish a “fossil fuel treaty”, vowed last week to use “all means necessary” to disrupt summer holidays.
A Metropolitan Police spokesman said: “At 08:48hrs on Thursday, Aug 1, officers at Heathrow airport became aware of protesters blocking a security lane at Terminal Five.
“Seven protesters were arrested on suspicion of interfering with key national infrastructure contrary to Section Seven of the Public Order Act 2023. They were taken to a west London police station, where they remain at this time. The incident was complete at 09:08hrs. Enquiries are ongoing.”
Just Stop Oil claimed two of the seven people arrested on Thursday were septuagenarians.
Di Bligh, 77, a former chief executive of Reading Borough council, and Ruth Cook, a 72-year-old from Somerset, were both said by the group to have been arrested by police.
In a prepared statement, Ms Bligh said: “Electric cars and windfarms won’t do it – governments must act together before we reach more tipping points into chaos than we can prevent.
“We need our political leaders to act now, by working with other nations to establish a legally binding treaty to stop the extraction and burning of oil, gas and coal by 2030.”
In a statement issued by Just Stop Oil, Ms Cook said: “I am here for my two grandchildren, my two grandnieces who have just come into this world, and for all children – what future will they face?
“I want to be able to look them in the eye and tell them that I did all that I could.”
The protest group claimed a total of 17 people had been arrested on Thursday morning, including 10 detained on public transport, six blocking travellers and one person filming the protesters.
It came the day after two of Just Stop Oil’s number were jailed for breaking their bail conditions. Phoebe Plummer, 22, and Jane Touil, 58, were remanded in custody on Wednesday after targeting Terminal Five in a similar protest on Tuesday.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: The response to the riots reflects terribly on our political class
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: The appalling scenes of violence across the country cannot be allowed to happen again
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
It should not be difficult to condemn, without equivocation, the violence we have seen on our streets in the past week. The perpetrators belong behind bars.
For the line between civilisation and chaos is thin, and public order is a public good too often taken for granted. Once lost, it can be difficult for the police to regain control, which is why the response to disorder must always be unequivocal and uncompromising, swift and tough.
Courts should, as the Government proposes, sit through the night, and judges must be prepared to hand down tough sentences, as they did to good effect during the riots of 2011. The police will need to use sophisticated capabilities – some covert, some utilising open-source information – to identify and round up rioters before the violence resumes.
On the streets, policing a violent crowd is a difficult and dangerous job, with the best tactics to restore order resembling those of medieval battles. Officers need to box the mob into confined spaces, and numbers, physical strength and a willingness to deploy force determine victory or loss. Exceptional circumstances dictate that leave be cancelled, officers called in to support affected areas, and rioters confronted with an overwhelming police presence.
Unfortunately, we live in a polarised age in which too many in positions of power let their politics trump the vital principle of equality before the law. On Friday, when Nigel Farage released a video saying he did not support the violence but added, “What you’ve seen on the streets of Hartlepool, of London, of Southport, is nothing to what could happen over the next few weeks”, he appeared to revel in anticipated vindication.
In condemning the “breakdown” of law and order preceding the riots, but not the riots themselves, and by failing to back the police officers dealing with the rioters, Farage flunked the test of leadership. Whatever you think about immigration or multiculturalism, there is no place in Britain for street violence. Almost all voters agree, but Farage sought not to use his position to quell the violence but to equivocate.
He is not alone. Nick Lowles – who runs Hope Not Hate, an advocacy group with the stated objective of promoting race equality – has said “those fanning the flames” are “just as guilty” as the rioters and should be investigated. But the day before, Lowles himself had promoted rumours on social media – declared to be without current basis by the local police – that acid had been thrown at a Muslim woman in Middlesbrough.
And the Prime Minister stands accused of advocating “two-tier policing”. Comparisons between the disorder this week and offences committed during the Black Lives Matter protests, the anti-Israel marches and so-called direct action by radical environmentalists are not precise. There is a difference between public protests in which some of the protesters turn violent, and disorder started deliberately by those intent on violence. There is a difference, too, between blocking a road and physically attacking people because of their race or religion.
Yet there is, nevertheless, some validity in the criticism. Starmer took the knee in support of BLM two days after the protests in London turned violent, leaving 27 police officers injured. He praised Extinction Rebellion for its disruptive protests and accepted party donations from Dale Vince, who helped bankroll Just Stop Oil. Labour MPs have consorted with organisations such as the Palestine Solidarity Campaign and Muslim Engagement and Development, known as Mend.
The police also deserve scrutiny. Officers were quick to act when campaigners wanted to protest at the King’s Coronation, but showed no such resolve in dealing with deliberately disruptive eco-protestors. When officers took the knee before BLM protestors, they later claimed privately that they had been encouraged to do so by their seniors. When, last year, an autistic boy was threatened by a mob for lightly scuffing a copy of the Koran, local police were present at a show trial held in a nearby mosque. The Met’s justification for not intervening when anti-Israel protestors appear to blatantly break the law is that they do not want to risk more serious public disorder. This is not policing “without fear or favour”.
All these examples – and now the latest disgraceful violence across England – should prompt us to ask sombre questions about what sort of society we have become. There is no future for a multiracial country in balkanising itself into a series of ethnic enclaves existing side by side but entirely separately from one another. And there is no time for us to continue the official denialism that dominates parts of the media and public sector.
For the policy of multiculturalism – of promoting difference between “communities” rather than national unity and shared citizenship under one civic identity – is visibly failing. As inter-ethnic tensions play out in cities from Leicester to Liverpool, sectarian politics enters the House of Commons, and the politicisation of white identity begins – with agitators promoting the grievance politics that appears to have borne fruit for extremists from other backgrounds – the failure is there for all to see. The recent tendency to sweep acts of extreme violence under the carpet, and to obfuscate about the identities and motives of the perpetrators, is now backfiring, manipulated by those who, in some cases knowingly, spread false information.
We should be honest about what all of this means for our future, and what we can do to change it now. The danger is that the Government – wedded to its belief in multiculturalism and abetted by the wider Left – continues the denialism and responds only in political fashion. Already, the signs are there that they see an opportunity to tar all those with mainstream conservative views – about immigration, violent crime and policing policy – with the same brush as the rioters and the instigators.
This would certainly be easier than confronting the true extent of our failure. A failure that can be seen in the burnt-out shops and vehicles strewn across our streets, and in the Rotherham hotel with migrants barricaded inside, but most damningly in the failure to properly mourn the appalling killing of three innocent little children.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Extinction Rebellion delivers pink postbox of letters for King to Windsor Castle
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: More than 500 activists marched through town centre on second day of protests
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Environmental protesters have delivered a bright pink postbox full of letters to King Charles at Windsor Castle urging him to help save the planet from ecological disaster.
More than 500 activists from Extinction Rebellion brought traffic to a standstill as they paraded through Windsor town centre on Saturday with the pink postbox at the head of the march.
Inside were handwritten messages from young and old urging the King to “intervene in the worsening climate crisis”.
On the postbox were printed last collection times of an apocalyptic nature, warning of the consequences of the imminent climate disaster – with food running short at 9am and floodwaters rising at 7pm.
Alongside the postbox activists carried banners quoting the King’s words back at him.
In a 2010 speech, the monarch, then Prince Charles, had declared: “This is a call for revolution. The Earth is under threat. Revolution is a strong word and I use it deliberately.”
The words resonated powerfully with the marchers, even if many would not consider themselves natural royalists.
Marigold, a financial services worker from the Midlands, told The Telegraph: “There are all sorts of people here, young and old, who have written to the King to tell him how strongly we feel about the climate and ecological emergency.”
As a troupe of Mayday Morris dancers danced beneath the statue of Queen Victoria, police formed a line in front of the gates where the marchers chanted “Extinction… Rebellion!” and “Democracy… Upgrade!” in a call for greater representation of people’s views.
Catherine Edminson, 61, a business support worker in the NHS, said: “All my colleagues in the NHS support XR. We’re facing a health crisis as a result of the ecological crisis and this is happening here and now in Britain.
“We’re not freaks. We come from all walks of society.”
As she spoke the figure of a yellow owl, an ancient symbol of wisdom and a warning from nature, sat impassively on the postbox.
Morag Sinton, 56, a council worker from Abergavenny, said: “We wrote our letter on the train down from a lovely part of Wales. We want the King to use his office to give everybody a voice and involve everyone in saving the planet.”
A mass assembly was also staged on Saturday on Windsor Great Park’s Long Walk, despite it not being given official permission to gather by the Crown Estate.
Participants were invited to speak and offer solutions and ideas for tackling the climate crisis.
Paul Thistlethwaite, a democracy facilitator from St Albans who helped set up the gathering, said: “This is about building solutions to society’s problems from the grassroots. It’s about giving everyone a voice and taking the power away from the elites.”
This was the second day of protests by XR, which has built an unauthorised encampment of tents and marquees on Windsor Home Park from where they have launched marches and eye-catching stunts and performances.
These included a symbolic oil slick composed of funereal figures dressed in black who filed slowly to the castle gates on Friday evening in a grim warning about the planet’s future.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: Former top Just Stop Oil donor turns on green campaigners
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: Dale Vince criticises ongoing protests after group’s demands were won ‘at the ballot box’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
The former Just Stop Oil (JSO) donor Dale Vince has criticised the group for becoming too extreme and said he does not support its push to end fossil extraction by 2030.
Mr Vince, who also gave £5m to Labour in the 12 months before the election, said that he backed the radical activist group when it was just attempting to prevent new drilling in the UK, but believes it has since gone too far.
However, he also criticised the long prison sentences handed to some campaigners, after a group was jailed for up to five years last month.
Mr Vince, who runs green energy provider Ecotricity, described the sentences as far too long. He added that he was “not a fan” of JSO’s new stance, or of its deployment of protesters trying to blockade airports.
It came as JSO announced on Wednesday that it was suspending all planned protests because of the riots across Britain.
Mr Vince said: “The aim has shifted from no new oil, because obviously Labour got elected on that platform, to ending the whole UK fossil fuel industry by 2030, and I don’t think that’s a sensible thing to ask for.
“I don’t think it’s a valid thing to make this kind of disruptive protest.
“I used to say, on the other side of the election … hopefully we just won’t need Just Stop Oil, because we’ll have stopped [new drilling for] oil through the ballot box by stopping the Tories.
“That was our campaign, just stop the Tories … there’s obviously no point disrupting now for no new licensing because that’s happening. We won that argument at the ballot box.”
Mr Vince is the founder and chief executive of Ecotricity, which supplies 100pc green electricity to 200,000 customers. In 2023 it declared a profit of £39m.
Mr Vince said setting a fixed date to abandon oil and gas was impractical because the UK was so far from being ready.
About 25m UK homes rely on gas boilers for heating and there are 32m petrol or diesel vehicles on the roads – with 30pc of UK electricity generated by gas-fired power stations.
Mr Vince said the UK had to move away from fossil fuels but the transition would take time.
He said: “There’s no point having an arbitrary cut-off for oil. We have to build like hell to the point that we just stop using it. That’s the logical thing to do.
“We’ve just got a Labor government with a massive majority, and a mandate for a green economy. And I’m surprised that there are protests going on within weeks of that, and that there’s a kind of ramping up of demands.
“I’m just surprised by that.”
Mr Vince said that he remained a staunch supporter of the right to protest – and attacked the sentences handed down to the JSO “Whole Truth Five”, as the group has become known.
Another 16 JSO protesters have also been jailed recently.
He called on Labour to change the laws and sentencing powers enshrined in the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022, which allow protesters to be charged with “conspiracy to cause a public nuisance” and given lengthy prison sentences simply for discussing future potential protests.
He said: “The right to protest seems to me to be fundamental, like the right to breathe air. It’s a way for people to call governments to account, policymakers and governments who are doing the wrong thing or aren’t listening.
“Back in the day the suffragettes were a pain in the a---. They took on the authorities with very direct, disruptive action but that’s how women got the vote.
“Similarly the ending of slavery was contentious in its time – the laws allowing slavery were challenged by activists who found themselves outside of moral norms and laws. But they were all right in the end.
“The Just Stop Oil protesters at the time [of the offence]  were spurred really, by the idea of halting drilling for new oil and gas in the North Sea, which is something that the United Nations has called economic and moral madness.
“And we all know that we can’t be drilling for new oil and gas. We’ve got plenty in the world. We don’t need it.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Protests prevent Met Police from tackling antisocial behaviour
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Inspectors warn that removing neighbourhood officers from their duties to deal with demonstrations is hurting force’s ability to fight crime
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Policing the protests in recent months has left the Metropolitan Police unable to tackle antisocial behaviour effectively, a highly critical report has found.
Inspectors warned that the constant “abstraction” of neighbourhood officers in the capital to deal with large-scale demonstrations was having a significant impact on the force’s ability to prevent and deter crime that was blighting people’s lives.
Officers described how they were unable to spend enough time on the beat or developing relationships with members of the public because they were constantly being diverted to other duties such as having to police large pro-Palestinian marches.
Since the Hamas terror attacks on Israel in October and the resulting conflict, pro-Palestinian supporters have held 16 large rallies in central London attended by tens of thousands of people.
In addition, action by environmental campaigners, including Just Stop Oil, has required a huge policing response from the Met.
The report, by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary, Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), warned that removing officers from their core roles to police protests meant communities were not getting the service they deserved from the force.
It stated: “Neighbourhood policing teams are responsible for problem-solving and getting local communities involved in crime prevention.
“But neighbourhood officers told us they couldn’t spend enough time carrying out visible patrols, working with the public, or doing preventative and problem-solving work. This is because they were often diverted to other non-neighbourhood duties.
“Abstracting neighbourhood officers from their core role has a negative effect on their work preventing crime and antisocial behaviour, meaning communities may not receive the service they require.”
It was one of a string of problems inspectors identified with the Met, which was placed in special measures two years ago following a series of scandals.
Inspectors who assessed Scotland Yard’s performance across eight areas of policing concluded it was inadequate in terms of investigating crime and managing offenders and required improvement in the areas of preventing crime; responding to the public; protecting vulnerable people; developing a positive workplace and its leadership and force management.
The report found that while the Met had made some progress in areas such as call handling, victims of crime were still being let down in a number of areas.
Lee Freeman, His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary, said there remained significant issues in the standard of some investigations, with cases involving vulnerable people being handed to inexperienced officers.
He warned that the number of wanted suspects in London had increased since the last inspection and the Met was inconsistent in the way it managed sex offenders – sometimes warning them before carrying out home visits.
The report accused the force of failing to consistently achieve good outcomes for victims of crime with just 3.1 per cent of the 789,544 offences resulting in a charge or a summons, down from 9.1 per cent in 2015.
Mr Freeman said: “The unique challenges facing the Metropolitan Police are not underestimated. Policing the capital city places additional strain on the force and its leadership, as the force tirelessly manages protests, state visits and royal occasions, and national and international sporting events.
“In parallel, the force is in the midst of an organisational-wide transformation, which is significant in both its size and scale. While it was evident in my inspection that many key changes have and are being made, they are not yet translating into consistent and sustained improvements in some key areas.
“While I commend the force for the progress it has made in answering the public’s calls quickly, I have serious concerns about how the force is currently investigating crime and how it manages offenders and suspects.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Police stand by as Extinction Rebellion protests at Windsor Castle
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Officers appear to just watch as activists erect dozens of tents
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Police in Windsor Great Park made no attempt to stop a mass protest from Extinction Rebellion activists at the Long Walk on Friday.
The marchers were allowed to assemble 500 metres from Windsor Castle’s gates, which is part of the Crown Estate – despite being earlier refused official permission to gather there.
After parading through Windsor town centre into the Great Park the accompanying drummers ceased playing and the march proceeded in silence to the assembly point.
Several dozen activists dressed as corporate stooges and representing the chocking effect of an oil slick on society and the environment assembled behind a banner facing Windsor Castle and declaring: “The System is Broken.”
Black-cloaked figures with ghostly white faces – like mourners at the planet’s funeral – filed slowly at the head of the main body of marchers.
It was intended by activists to be interpreted as a dramatic metaphor of oil choking the environment in spills at sea and released into the atmosphere as carbon emissions.
Behind them, the marchers moved to a slow beat, a death march filing towards the castle gates.
Earlier, officers had appeared to stand and watch as activists erected dozens of tents in Windsor Home Park with Extinction Rebellion (XR) flags and a green banner, which read “Upgrade Democracy” in Windsor Home Park, where they were encamped.
As the protesters waited to begin the short stroll to the castle gates overlooking Long Walk, where a symbolic re-enactment of a devastating oil slick was being staged, teams of police officers wandered discreetly through the camp, keeping an eye on the preparations and relaying information back to their control centre.
In the town centre, drummers and marchers were greeted by a mixture of bemusement, smiles and cheers, along with a few jeers, as they made their way past shoppers and tourists.
Small groups of police officers stood at junctions along the route as the protesters filed past, happy to give directions to Windsor Castle when asked.
Officials from Windsor and Maidenhead council made sure nothing untoward was being done to the Home Park’s fields and sports pitches, sighted half a mile from the castle.
But although the camp is unauthorised, the Liberal Democrat-controlled council appeared to have taken the decision not to enforce any ban or evict those taking part.
By mid-afternoon the number of tents had swelled to nearly 100, bordered by a row of colourful flags and placards with drawings of bees, trees, swallows and turtles, alongside the ubiquitous Extinction Rebellion symbol of an X within a circle.
The impression was of a mini-Glastonbury, but without the music, the chatter of activists periodically drowned out by aircraft flying overhead along the Heathrow flight path.
Food was being served in a large open-sided marquee set up for the weekend.
The public was warned to stay away from Long Walk this weekend as thousands of protesters began erecting tents in the shadow of Windsor Castle.
Signs have been put up around Windsor Great Park advising tourists and visitors that activists from XR were planning to stage a weekend-long protest along the famous Long Walk.
Police have erected high steel barriers in front of the gates to Windsor Castle to deter any attempts to climb into the Royal family’s private grounds.
XR has denied any such plans, but there are fears that more radical elements among the protesters could attempt to scale the gates and reach the castle.
The notices stated that although the protest has been banned by the Windsor Great Park authorities, it is still likely to go ahead.
They read: “While we have not given consent to this protest, parts of the protest may be located on The Long Walk.
“It is possible that large crowds may attend the protest which could be disruptive to other visitors. Please be vigilant and consider avoiding the Long Walk area during these times.”
The Long Walk, which runs through Windsor Great Park, has been used for royal parades and processions over decades, including the wedding of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.
It is seen by XR as the perfect location to generate publicity with what it has described as a mass assembly, or “Massembly”, which it claims could be “one of the largest participatory, democratic events ever held in the UK”.
The group, which advocates non-violent direct action and civil disobedience, vowed the protests would go ahead as planned, despite the objections of Windsor and Maidenhead council and the Crown Estate.
As part of the three-day protests, activists were staging a symbolic re-enactment by black-clad protesters of “oil slicks”, signifying “how our political, judicial and media systems now serve the interests of oil, money, and other villains”.
Shortly after 5pm, the protesters began moving in small groups towards Windsor Castle, accompanied by two dozen synchronised drummers.
With them were activists dressed as businessmen and corporate executives, brandishing placards reading: “Regulate nothing”, “Politicians are our puppets” and “Money is our God”.
Etienne Stott, the spokesman of XR UK and Olympic gold medal-winning canoeist, said: “The first job of the state is to protect its citizens and keep them safe. Politicians are too close to and too compromised by the vested interests of the oil barons and media billionaires to carry out this primary duty of care. A citizens’ assembly is a proven mechanism that can be deployed to bypass these corrupting influences and get things done in a way that is fair for all and bridges political divides.”
The group, whose offshoot Just Stop Oil has occupied and blockaded dozens of locations in recent years, including the M25, denied it planned to invade the grounds of Windsor Castle but promised “exciting plans to fix the current broken system”.
Marijn van de Geer, of XR UK’s Citizens Assembly Working Group, said: “Extinction Rebellion UK does not have any plans to storm Windsor Castle, any hotels, nor cause public disruption during our three-day event ‘Upgrade Democracy’ in Windsor.
“But we will be hatching exciting plans to fix the current broken system that is burning down the planet. This gathering is about uniting communities for positive change, not disruption or alienation.”
In a statement, Windsor and Maidenhead council said: “Having previously made it clear that Extinction Rebellion do not have permission for a festival with overnight camping in Home Park, we are aware that they have begun to arrive in the area.
“We are continuing to engage with the organisers, having made it clear that their plans for a festival with overnight camping in Home Park do not have permission. We will continue to monitor the situation with our partners Thames Valley Police, and the Crown Estate to ensure the safety of those in attendance and take action where needed.”
Throughout the planned events the canteen marquee at the centre of the XR encampment was continuing to serve a hearty selection of salads and accompaniments, from organic tomatoes to mung beans and grated carrots with raisins.
Also on the menu was tahini and pita bread, with a lentil stew topped off with sweet chilli sauce and a mango chutney.
Over lunch – which was served at plain wooden trestle tables on an assortment of multicoloured plastic plates with wooden cutlery – those taking part discussed strategy.
“How do we attract young people?” asked one middle-aged lady.
“Young people will do what they want to do,” replied her companion. “This is for us and anyone else who wants to join in.”
In the queue, another middle-aged participant was discussing the day’s slogans.
“Is ‘XR: The Revolution Starts Here’ a bit too much?” he pondered aloud. “No, no. I love that,” said a young woman behind him, as a generous portion of tamari glazed nuts and tahini was ladled onto her plate. “It suits the mood. We are serious about this, even while we’re still having fun.”
While they ate, others queued to do the washing up, cleaning their plates in two large bowls – one with washing up liquid, one full of clean water for rinsing.
Behind them, children ran around playing chase, oblivious to the group of protesters lying on the grass at a seminar on the tactics of non-violent direct action, XR’s guiding tactics for protest.
Mr Stott told The Telegraph: “We’re a very diverse group of people, of all ages, beliefs, causes and social backgrounds.
“We’re not interested in disrupting anyone’s day or targeting the King or storming the castle. Our protests are a form of education. We’re putting forward the idea of a people’s assembly of representative citizens to upgrade democracy and tackle the climate crisis that threatens our society and our planet in a far more urgent way than traditional political systems are doing.”
Behind him stood tents assigned to various functions, including the citizens’ assembly information tent, the treasury (for donations) and the talks and training tent.
Back in the marquee, the last of the lentil stew was being served along with a replenished bowl of fresh lettuce and tomatoes. All organic of course. King Charles would feel very much at home.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.title: Extinction Rebellion plans to occupy Windsor Castle grounds
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.subtitle: Activists plan to create diversion with protesters in fancy dress on Long Walk, allowing others to slip into out of bounds areas
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/08.text:
Extinction Rebellion (XR) is encouraging elderly supporters to take part in mass demonstrations in which the group plans to occupy restricted areas of Windsor Castle’s grounds, according to a report by security analysts.
The climate change protesters are planning three days of action at Windsor Great Park, the site of one of the King’s main residences.
The grounds of the castle are also home to Adelaide Cottage, where the Princess of Wales has spent time recuperating from cancer.
Activists plan to create a diversion with protesters in fancy dress on the park’s Long Walk, allowing others to slip into areas that are out of bounds to the public, according to security documents seen by The Telegraph.
The information was revealed after private investigators, acting on behalf of a local businesses, reportedly infiltrated online discussions by XR activists.
In an online discussion, members of the XR leadership team said they wanted to make the protest “as inclusive as possible”, extending to elderly and disabled activists, according to the report by ASG Pivotal.
XR leadership members pointed out that elderly and disabled activists can contribute to the success of direct action. Others affiliated with the group said the optics of removing elderly or disabled activists were “extremely challenging” for the police.
The report also said activists affiliated with XR had discussed plans to target hotels and restaurants in Windsor town centre, while blocking local roads.
But in a statement XR said it “does not have any plans to storm Windsor Castle, any hotels, nor cause public disruption during our three-day ‘Upgrade Democracy’ event in Windsor.
The statement said: “We won’t be storming any castles – but we will be hatching exciting plans to fix the current broken system that is burning down the planet.”
Marijn van de Geer, of XR, added that the gathering was “about uniting communities for positive change, not disruption or alienation”.
XR got permission for a three-day mass demonstration within the park, and cited King Charles’s commitment to environmental causes when it was announced last month. The organisation’s Catherine Bartlett said: “Windsor Castle has been chosen as an embodiment of a broken and unjust system, where our message will resonate powerfully.”
Windsor Castle was considered the main residence of the late Queen, and her remains are interred in the King George VI Memorial chapel on the grounds, alongside her husband.
The chapel and parts of the grounds are usually open to ticket-holding members of the public during the summer months, including the days of planned protests from Aug 30 to Sep 1.
The King and Queen are currently in Scotland, while the Prince and Princess of Wales are at their residence in Norfolk but are expected to return to Windsor in time for the start of the school year on Sept 4.
Former Olympic canoeist Etienne Stott is among the leading organisers of the protest, because of his links to the local area including the nearby Dorney Lakes, where he trained for the 2012 London Games.
The report said: “Activists will be meeting at The Long Walk to carry out that mass trespass into Windsor Castle Grounds at 6pm.
“Activists have been asked to dress in business suits or as oil barons – there will be the XR red and black brigade doing their pageantry on the Long Walk itself. However, this will be a choreographed distraction to allow other activists to attempt to mass trespass into restricted areas of Windsor Castle grounds.
“Should this be prevented or dispersed, online chatter suggested targeting local businesses that serve high net worth individuals as secondary targets. Several high-end hotels were mentioned as part of this list. So those in the local area should be vigilant Friday early evening.”
Thames Valley Police said it would not stop the demonstration going ahead but that criminal activity would be dealt with quickly.
A spokesman for the force said: “Thames Valley Police is aware of a planned demonstration in Windsor from Aug 30 until Sep 1. We have been in contact with the organisers and are working closely with partners to put a comprehensive plan in place to facilitate peaceful protest and ensure the safety of all those in attendance and other members of the public.
“We will not tolerate criminal behaviour, and those choosing to commit offences can expect to be dealt with swiftly and robustly.”
Windsor Council said plans by XR to extend the three days of protests to include overnight camping and a festival had been denied permission.
A council spokesman said: “While we recognise Extinction Rebellion’s central message on addressing the climate emergency, and respect the right for peaceful protest, we have a responsibility to ensure that any proposed event is planned appropriately and consider any impact on our residents and businesses.
“We have engaged with the organisers and made it clear that their advertised plan for a festival and overnight camping in Home Park does not have permission.
“They have accepted this, and we expect them to amend their plans.”
XR said it had no plans to scale back its protests.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.title: Yvette Cooper set to revive tough anti-protest laws introduced by Suella Braverman
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.subtitle: Looser definitions of ‘serious disruption’ could lead to swifter and stricter punishments for activists
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Yvette Cooper will seek to revive Suella Braverman’s tough anti-protest laws designed to crack down on groups like Just Stop Oil.
The Home Secretary is to appeal against a High Court ruling that quashed the laws after civil rights group Liberty challenged their legality.
The new laws allowed the police to impose restrictions on protests where there was merely a “more than minor” hindrance on people’s daily lives.
It lowered the threshold which had previously only permitted police curbs where there was a risk of “serious disruption.”
The new law was introduced through a statutory instrument in the Lords after peers had previously rejected the same change, proposed months earlier in a new public order act.
Peers do not by convention normally vote down statutory instruments.
Hundreds of protesters including climate activist Greta Thunberg have been arrested since the looser definition of “serious disruption” was introduced.
Liberty won a legal challenge against the Home Office in May over the regulations after it argued it was unlawful as it had already been democratically rejected by Parliament just a few months earlier. It said bringing it back “via the back door” through “secondary legislation” allowed less Parliamentary scrutiny and debate.
The High Court found that the Government had failed to undertake a fair consultation period, instead only inviting thoughts from those it knew would be supportive of its proposals, such as the police but not protest groups.
It agreed with Liberty’s arguments, ruling that “more than minor cannot mean serious”.
The Home Office has now said it will appeal the ruling. It is understood that it is concerned at the impact that the judicial review could have on the ability of the Government to conduct consultations in future.
If the Home Office appeal is successful, the law would be revived.
The Government has pledged to carry out a review of the protest legislation next year, which could lead to changes. Labour politicians raised concerns about aspects of the legislation’s impact on rights to protest when the party was in opposition.
Akiko Hart, Liberty’s director, said: “We are very disappointed that, despite a positive discussion about the impact of the unlawful regulation, the Home Secretary has taken the decision to continue this case. This legislation is undemocratic, unconstitutional and unacceptable.
“The Home Office’s decision to continue the case shows disregard for the rule of law and completely goes against previous statements from the Government just last month that they would not abuse the use of secondary legislation and that they would promote high standards of governance.
“With hundreds of people wrongfully arrested and convicted due to this unlawful legislation already, it is not right to continue to carry on with this law that should never have been made in the first place. The only right thing to do would be to quash this legislation once and for all.”
A Home Office spokesman said: “The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy, and all public order legislation must balance this right.
“However, we disagree with the court’s ruling in this case and have appealed their decision.”
